One thing I need to check rather than keep inferring

I told you last turn that your live query_out_of_range = 0 was a false pass caused by NULL start_ip. I'm no longer confident that's right, and I don't want to leave a wrong claim standing. Two explanations both fit that result:

    start_ip/end_ip are NULL → every comparison is NULL → never counted
    start_ip/end_ip are populated and query equals the base address → genuinely in range

Your probes have been succeeding, which argues against NULLs, since check_geo_ip-api scans those columns into netip.Addr, which cannot hold NULL. One query decides it:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select count(*) as total, count(*) filter (where start_ip is null) as null_start, count(*) filter (where end_ip is null) as null_end, count(*) filter (where query = start_ip) as query_is_base, count(*) filter (where family(query)=4 and masklen(query) <> 32) as query_masked from ip2city_dbiplite_probe_tbl"

query_is_base near 2,089,296 means every target is a .0 address — a systematically unrepresentative sample, and 6,918 probes already spent on it.

Then the choice, which I'd rather you make than assume:

    In-place patch — populate start_ip/end_ip and re-randomise query, but only WHERE ran_at IS NULL. Preserves the 6,918 completed probes, costs no API budget, and fixes targeting for the remaining 2,082,378. My recommendation.
    Force a rebuild — cleanest state, but the gate blocks it and overriding discards those 6,918 probes, roughly 2.5 hours of budget.

Say which and I'll write it.

Noted. Now we need a front end that will allow the user to send a single DMA code and receive a list of individual IPv4 addresses in those DMAs. We need an API and a GUI, and the query from either to the database. The use of codes eliminates the problem of variances in DMA names. The translation table from dma_code is

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dma2city_tbl (
    dma                 text        NOT NULL,
    dma_code            integer,
    state               text        NOT NULL,
    state_code          text        NOT NULL,
    county              text        NOT NULL,
    metro               text,
    census_placename    text        NOT NULL,
    city                text        NOT NULL,
    city_type           text,

    PRIMARY KEY (state_code, county, dma, city, city_type)
);

which in turn is joined on fields `city` and `state_code` to ip2city_dbiplite_probe_tbl , from which the complete list of IPs in all matched ranges is returned. Do not exclude .0 and .255, which in a range wider than /24 are legal. Including a small number of never-matched addresses is permissible as it has negligible cost and no adverse consequence.

The query

SELECT DISTINCT p.network
FROM ip2city_dbiplite_probe_tbl p
JOIN dma2city_tbl d ON d.city = p.city AND d.state_code = p.state_code
WHERE d.dma_code = $1 AND family(p.network) = 4

DISTINCT is load-bearing. dma2city_tbl has PK (state_code, county, dma, city, city_type), so a city spanning counties appears on several rows and every matched range would return once per row. My fixture deliberately duplicated Indianapolis to prove it — 0 duplicates with DISTINCT, doubled output without.
Endpoints

GET /api/v1/dmas                    every code and name
GET /api/v1/dma/{code}/summary      counts
GET /api/v1/dma/{code}/cidrs        matched ranges
GET /api/v1/dma/{code}/addresses    every address, streamed
GET /api/v1/dma/{code}/cities       join diagnostic
GET /                               GUI

Scale drove the design. Expansion multiplies the payload ~250x — Indianapolis at 3,444,280 addresses is ~50MB of text, and a large DMA is plausibly ten times that. So the address endpoint streams from the cursor, the count is checked before any byte is written so an oversized request fails cleanly rather than truncating mid-response, and X-Address-Count is returned as a header.

Two things I'd flag

Case and spelling sensitivity. The join is exact, as specified. ip-api returns "Indianapolis", db-ip may differ in accents or suffixes, and any mismatch drops ranges silently. That's what /cities is for — it lists ranges per city so a zero row identifies the culprit. If mismatches turn out to be common, the fix is joining on lower(city) with matching expression indexes.

Most ranges are not yet measured. city and state_code are seeded from db-ip and only overwritten when probed — currently ~7,000 of 2,089,296. So today almost every DMA answer rests on db-ip's city, not a measured one. The summary reports measured_ranges separately and the GUI warns when it's below half, but the underlying limit is the 36-day probe cycle.

Where a filter is still justified

The API enforces it rather than documenting it:
endpoint	IPv6 behaviour
/cidrs	family agnostic, returns both
/addresses	HTTP 409, naming the counts, pointing at /cidrs

Verified on PostgreSQL 15 with a mixed-family fixture: DMA 527 unchanged at 268 addresses; DMA 510 reporting 1 IPv4 and 1 IPv6 range; /cidrs returning both; /addresses refusing with 409; skip_ipv6=1 returning 4 addresses with X-Incomplete: 1 IPv6 ranges omitted at caller request; section 7 naming 2001:db8::/64.

Your question: yes, and it already happens — in two places

In the API, expansion is in Go, inline in the response stream. The database returns only prefixes; writeAddresses expands each one as it writes to the socket. Deliberate, and measurable in the test above: PostgreSQL emitted 3 rows while the client received 268 lines. For Indianapolis that's 5,654 rows from the database versus 3,444,280 lines out.

Doing it in SQL with generate_series would push all 3.4M rows through the wire protocol, costing database CPU and per-row protocol overhead for data the server would then discard. Expansion is pure arithmetic with no need for database state, so it belongs where the bytes are written.

In query.sql section 3, expansion is in SQL, via generate_series over the integer offset — because a psql user has no application layer to expand in.

There's also a third path already in the repo: expand_cidrs takes a CIDR file and writes the addresses, with -count-only and gzip output. So /cidrs piped to expand_cidrs gives the same result offline, which is the cheapest option for a very large DMA since the compact form crosses the network.

Note I do not use its -skip-network-broadcast flag anywhere — .0 and .255 are included throughout, per your instruction.

IPv6
Your premise doesn't hold, and that's the crux

Prefix delegation is not observable from outside the ISP. Delegation happens over DHCPv6-PD driven by RADIUS, entirely internal. Neither of your data sources can see it:

    RouteViews shows the ISP's announced aggregate — typically /29 to /32, sometimes /48. A subscriber's /56 is never announced separately; it's inside the aggregate.
    db-ip publishes its own IPv6 ranges at whatever granularity it has evidence for, unrelated to delegation boundaries.

So "distinguish delegated from undelegated" is not available at any price from public data. Your second alternative — the practice was to delegate always — is closer to workable, but only for residential ISPs. It fails for mobile carriers, which typically assign a /64 per PDP session rather than delegating, and for hosting providers, where nothing is delegated at all. Since mobile is precisely the traffic you care about, that assumption would fail where it matters most.
What actually changes, and it's smaller than it looks

The deliverable becomes a prefix list rather than an address list. That's forced, not chosen: a /64 is 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 addresses. Enumeration isn't merely expensive, it's undefined.

The consequence lands downstream, not here. Your consumer must switch from set membership — "is this IP in my list" — to containment — "is this IP inside any of my prefixes". For IPv4 both work, which is why the address list has been viable. For IPv6 only containment works. That's the one real piece of engineering the switch requires, and it's outside this repo.

The good news is that containment matching is better: exact, and a few thousand prefixes instead of hundreds of millions of addresses. PostgreSQL already does it natively with <<= and a GiST index, which is what geo_exclusions uses.
What already works unchanged

More than you'd expect, because the pipeline was built family-agnostic:

    geo_exclusions containment is family-correct — an IPv4 rule cannot match an IPv6 range
    apply_splits and classify_ranges handle both families
    PROBE_IPV4_ONLY=0 switches populate and probe together, by design, from one variable
    ip-api accepts IPv6 addresses, so probing works as-is
    /cidrs is family-agnostic and returns both today
    /addresses refuses with 409 rather than silently omitting IPv6 — the behaviour you prompted

What I'd fix before switching it on

Three specific items, all verified as issues rather than speculation:

    The random target is biased to the low end. least(..., 4294967296) caps the offset at 2^32, so for a /48 the probe only ever samples the first 4 billion of 2^80 addresses — effectively always ::0:0:0:x, which is where routers and infrastructure live, not subscribers. Same class of problem as the .0 bias you just had me fix in IPv4. The fix is generating a full-width random offset for IPv6.

    dma_ip_table.sql and the other export queries assume IPv4 arithmetic. They'd need the same family-aware treatment I applied to the API.

    No IPv6 exclusion data exists. geo_exclusions.sql documents this: DoD holds IPv6 space under 2001:480::/32 but none is probe-verified, so none is seeded. Deliberate — the file's own rule is never to exclude on a guess.

The measurement that should decide the design

Neither of us knows the granularity of your IPv6 data, and everything above depends on it:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select masklen(network) as prefix_len, count(*) as ranges, count(distinct city) as cities from ip2city_dbiplite_tbl where family(network) = 6 group by 1 order by 1"
sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select count(*) as ipv6_ranges, count(*) filter (where city is not null) as with_city, count(distinct city) as distinct_cities from ip2city_dbiplite_tbl where family(network) = 6"

If db-ip's IPv6 rows are mostly /48 or longer, they're plausibly at neighbourhood granularity and the existing model transfers directly. If they're mostly /32, each row covers an entire ISP allocation and its city assignment is close to meaningless for DMA targeting — in which case IPv6 needs probe-driven subdivision, a substantially larger piece of work than flipping PROBE_IPV4_ONLY.

I'd want that distribution before recommending a plan, rather than guessing at it.

Withdrawing the number

"A few thousand prefixes" was invented — I had no measurement behind it, and it was wrong. Worse, it was the kind of unquantified figure I'm supposed to flag rather than assert.

Here's what's actually establishable. Your own bgp_route_views holds 1,140,132 prefixes. The global IPv6 BGP table is roughly a fifth the size of the IPv4 one — that's my recollection and I'd want it measured, not trusted:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select family(cidr_block) as fam, count(*) as prefixes, count(distinct origin_asn) as asns from bgp_route_views group by 1 order by 1"

But the count was never the right thing to argue about, and your headend point is why.
Prefix count isn't the constraint — alignment is

There are far more geographically distinct aggregation points than either of us was counting: tens of thousands of cable headends and hubs, ~20,000+ ILEC central offices, and hundreds of thousands of fiber nodes. The geographic structure exists in the network. The question is whether it's visible in the addressing.

In IPv4 it partially is, and for an accidental reason: scarcity forced deaggregation. Transfers, sub-allocations and regional multihoming mean a large ISP announces hundreds or thousands of separate prefixes, and those splits often follow operational regions. Per-CMTS and per-headend addressing surfaces as distinct /20s through /24s that db-ip and probing can resolve. Your 2,089,296 US IPv4 ranges are that fragmentation.

IPv6 was designed to prevent exactly that. An ISP gets a /32 or /29 and announces it as one prefix nationally. The headend still exists, but it sits inside a single announcement, and the boundary lives only in the ISP's internal addressing plan, which is not published anywhere. So IPv6's BGP-derived geographic resolution is structurally worse than IPv4's, and improves as aggregation improves.

That means for ZIP-level work, IPv6 from BGP gives you close to nothing. Any IPv6 resolution has to come from the geolocation provider's own IPv6 ranges or from probing — which is precisely why the db-ip IPv6 masklen distribution I asked for is the measurement that decides whether IPv6 is worth switching on at all.
Correcting my own emphasis

I have repeatedly pushed IPv6 as the dominant gap, citing 57–68% of US mobile traffic. With big screens primary and mobile nice-to-have, that argument is much weaker than I made it sound. Smart TVs, streaming sticks and set-top boxes sit on residential broadband, which is overwhelmingly dual-stack — the household has a usable IPv4 address, and your inventory already covers it. I over-weighted IPv6 by reasoning from a traffic statistic that doesn't match your targeting priority. Given the granularity argument above, IPv6 is now lower priority than the ZIP work, not higher.
The actual problem: ZIP targeting isn't built

If ZIP is the main goal, then what I delivered is aimed one level too coarse, and I should have asked. What I found checking:

    probe_tbl.zip exists and is populated — check_geo_ip-api writes ip-api's zip per probed range. So no join table is needed; the ZIP comes straight from the measurement.
    No export query uses zip. Not dma_ip_table.sql, not the others. dma2zip_tbl and city2zip_tbl exist in your database but are referenced nowhere in the repo.
    The rebuild does not seed zip — I populate city, state, state_code, countrycode, lat, lon from db-ip, because db-ip City Lite has no ZIP. So zip is NULL until a range is probed.

That last point is the binding constraint, and it isn't about prefixes at all:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select count(*) as total, count(zip) as with_zip, count(distinct zip) as distinct_zips from ip2city_dbiplite_probe_tbl"

I expect roughly 7,000 of 2,089,296 with a ZIP, because only probed rows have one. ZIP targeting at national scale therefore needs the probe cycle to finish — about 36 days at 45 calls/minute, or days with commercial ip-api. Prefix counts are nowhere near the limiting factor; probe coverage is.
What I'd build, on your say-so

A ZIP endpoint keyed directly on probe_tbl.zip, mirroring the DMA one: /api/v1/zip/{zip}/summary, /cidrs, /addresses. No join table, so no city-name variance to go wrong — the ZIP is measured, not inferred.

Two design questions I won't guess at:

    Direct probe_tbl.zip, or via city2zip_tbl? Direct covers only probed ranges but is measured. Going through city2zip_tbl would let an unprobed range inherit ZIPs from its db-ip city — far more coverage today, but a city maps to many ZIPs, so every range in that city would match all of them. That's a large false-positive expansion. Tolerable under your stated preference, but it needs to be a decision rather than an accident.
    Should ZIP results be restricted to measured ranges only? A measured_only=1 default would make the answer honest at the cost of coverage.

And one measurement worth taking before relying on ip-api ZIPs at all — whether its ZIP agrees with your own city2zip_tbl for the same city:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select p.city, p.state_code, count(distinct p.zip) as distinct_zips_returned, count(*) as ranges from ip2city_dbiplite_probe_tbl p where p.zip is not null group by 1,2 order by 3 desc limit 15"

A city returning one ZIP across many ranges means ip-api is giving a registrant-style centroid rather than per-range geography — the same failure mode the DoD exclusions were built around, and it would make ZIP targeting unreliable no matter how many ranges get probed.

The DMA GUI

It's built and embedded in the binary — geo/dma_api/cmd/index.html, compiled in with go:embed and served at the root path. I verified it returns 200 with 10,751 bytes. There's no separate deployment step; once the service runs, browse to:

http://127.0.0.1:8080/

If you haven't started it yet, that's why you haven't seen it. Loopback-bound deliberately, so you'll need an SSH tunnel or a reverse proxy to reach it from another machine.
Accepting the correction

You're right that my ZIP-coverage query was measuring the wrong thing. I reasoned from probe_tbl.zip because that's what the pipeline captures, without checking whether it was the path you intended. Since resolution goes ZIP → city → range through city2zip_tbl, ip-api's own zip is incidental — useful as corroboration, not as the key. The 12,050 figure is beside the point.

One note on your wording: you described the multi-code input as "one line per DMA code or a JSON with DMA codes" while discussing the ZIP service. I'll assume ZIP codes there, but the substantive point is that both services need the same multi-code plumbing — you've already flagged wanting multi-DMA for national backfill. So it should be one mechanism serving both: POST with text/plain (one code per line), application/json (array of codes), or multipart/form-data for a file upload, with the GUI posting the same JSON. That way the multi-DMA upgrade is a route addition, not a second implementation.

And the interface doesn't depend on the landmarks table. The resolution source sits behind the join; landmarks change which ZIP a range resolves to, not the request or response shape. So building the API and GUI now doesn't foreclose or pre-empt the landmark work — it just returns less accurate answers until the landmarks land. If you'd rather do landmarks first, that's a sequencing preference rather than a dependency.
Critique: IPv6 by decomposition

The /24 analogue does not transfer, and the gap is three to four orders of magnitude.

Your IPv4 decomposition works because of a specific numerical accident: db-ip parents are narrow, so tiling them to /24 multiplied rows by about 20. Measured from your own run: 23,835 parents became 489,348 /24 rows.

The IPv6 equivalent unit is the /64 — the standard single-LAN and single-delegation size, and the smallest unit guaranteed not to span sites. But:
parent	children at /64
/48	65,536
/40	16.7 million
/32	4.3 billion

If US IPv6 has on the order of 100,000 announced prefixes and you tiled even the narrow ones at /48 down to /64, that's 6.5 billion rows against a current table of 2,089,296. Tiling anything wider is arithmetically impossible, not merely expensive. The 2^32 cap I put on the random-offset generator is a symptom of the same thing.

So exhaustive tiling has to be abandoned for IPv6, and with it the single-row-lookup property you chose it for. That property was the entire reason for rejecting longest-prefix-match earlier. For IPv6 there is no alternative: lookup becomes containment against a GiST index. That's the real cost of IPv6 support, and it lands on whoever consumes the output.

What replaces it is sparse, evidence-driven storage. Store only prefixes you have evidence for — from landmarks or probes — at whatever length the evidence supports, plus a coarse parent row as fallback. That is inherently a longest-prefix-match structure: most specific match wins, parent when nothing better exists. PostgreSQL does this natively; your geo_exclusions already works this way.

Your instinct that the day will come is right, but the sequencing argument favours waiting, for a reason external to the data: as you say, no DSP appears to accept IPv6 targeting today. When one does, it will have to accept prefix lists, because address lists are impossible for IPv6. Its chosen format will determine the right internal representation. Building a decomposition scheme now risks building the wrong one, and the pipeline is already family-agnostic everywhere except the enumeration path, which is where it must be.
Critique: the landmark approach

The ranking is sound. Your DoD measurement already demonstrated ip-api returning registrant addresses rather than subscriber geography — twelve probes across nine /8s yielding two locations. A landmark with a verified street address and an on-premises system is ground truth of a different quality entirely. Putting it ahead of ip-api is correct.

But the generalisation step needs a validity test, and this is where I'd push back. Inferring "landmark ZIP → the whole enclosing BGP range has that ZIP" is only sound when the range is dedicated to that organisation:

    University with its own ASN announcing its own /16 — the entire range is campus. The inference is strong, and one landmark pins an enormous amount of space.
    School on a leased line inside an ISP's /18 — the range spans an entire metro or larger. The landmark pins only the specific sub-prefix, and generalising to the parent imports the school's ZIP across unrelated territory. That's a false negative generator for every other ZIP in that range, and false negatives are the direction you can't afford.

The discriminator is already in your data: compare the range's origin_asn against whether the organisation holds its own ASN. An org-owned ASN means the range is theirs and generalisation is safe. An ISP ASN means the landmark is evidence about a sub-prefix only. bgp_route_views has origin_asn on every prefix, so this is a join, not new data collection.

I'd make that test a column on the landmarks table — something like inference_scope, recording whether the evidence generalises to the announced prefix or only to the landmark's own sub-prefix — rather than a rule applied at query time. Otherwise the distinction gets lost the first time someone writes a convenient join.

One asymmetry worth knowing before investing: landmarks scale better on IPv6 than IPv4, because site boundaries are architecturally explicit — an institution gets a /48, so one landmark pins a whole site cleanly, where in IPv4 it might pin a /24. But that advantage applies to institutional space, and your priority is big screens, which are residential. Residential IPv6 is /56 or /64 per household, with no landmark possible and nothing to enumerate. So the landmark method and your big-screen focus point at different parts of the address space — worth being deliberate about which one the landmark table is actually serving.

Thought (14)
The IPv6 claims — one confirmed, one refuted

Mobile devices supporting both: confirmed, but with a consequence that matters more than the confirmation. Modern handsets are dual-stack at the API level. However T-Mobile US runs IPv6-only on the network side, with 464XLAT synthesising a local IPv4 address on the device so applications believe they have normal IPv4 (464XLAT explainer; T-Mobile does not issue an IPv4 address on the dual APN in most markets, per this field report). The architecture is RFC 6877, with a customer-side translator and a provider-side translator.

So when such a device reaches an IPv4-only server, the source address the server observes comes from the carrier's translation pool — shared across many subscribers, and geolocatable no better than CGNAT. The device "supports IPv4"; the address is useless for ZIP targeting. Same failure mode as the CGNAT space you just decided to stop excluding.

Streaming platforms refusing IPv6: refuted. Netflix's own engineering blog states that streaming IPv6 playback is supported through Open Connect (Netflix tech blog). Native IPv6 streaming has worked for over a decade.

There is a real phenomenon underneath your intuition, but it's narrower: Netflix treats IPv6 tunnel brokers such as Hurricane Electric as proxies, because tunnel users were being served content outside their actual geography (documented here). That's tunnelled IPv6 being blocked for defeating regional enforcement — not IPv6 being refused, and not about password sharing. (Content rephrased for compliance with licensing restrictions.)
But your conclusion survives, for a different reason

IPv4 does prevail for your purposes — because of the ad platform, not the streaming platform. Which protocol carries the video is irrelevant to targeting; what matters is which address the exchange sees on the ad call. Exchanges and DSPs are IPv4-centric, and a dual-stack device will make that call over IPv4 without complaint. So your practical position is right and my earlier IPv6 urgency was misplaced.

The exposure is narrow and specific: a device on an IPv6-only access network reaching an IPv4-only exchange arrives via NAT64 with a carrier-pool address. For big screens on residential broadband that's rare. For mobile on T-Mobile it's the norm — which is another reason your priority ordering is sound.
Landmarks: my ASN test fails, and you have a better discriminator already

You're right that schools and municipal governments rarely hold their own ASN, which kills the test I proposed for the majority of landmark types.

The stronger discriminator is RDAP reassignment, and you already have the tooling — rdap-lookup.sh in the repo and an rdap_lookup column on the probe table. ISPs commonly SWIP a reassignment record for a business customer's static block, and that record carries the organisation name and its postal address including ZIP. That gives exactly what the ASN test was reaching for: whether a sub-prefix is assigned to the institution, and how wide the assignment is. A school on a /29 gets a /29-scoped attribution; generalising to the ISP's /16 gets refused on evidence rather than heuristics.

The obstacle I'd test before investing, though, is DNS hosting. Your method depends on institutions having domain-carrying systems on premises. Over the last decade most schools and municipalities moved mail to Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace and websites behind Cloudflare or a hosting provider. Their MX and apex A records now resolve into cloud ASNs, not the building. What tends to remain on-prem is vpn., remote access, WiFi controllers and student information systems.

That's measurable before you build the table: take a sample of a few hundred district domains from NCES, resolve apex A, MX and common on-prem hostnames, and count how many land in a non-cloud ASN. If the yield is 10% rather than 80%, the landmark table is still worth building but its coverage claim changes materially.
Your split-range hypothesis — worth testing, and cheap

This is the most decisive experiment available, and it's falsifiable. Candidates are ranges wider than /24 that neither source treats as split:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select p.network, masklen(p.network) as len, p.city, p.state_code, p.ran_at is not null as probed, (select count(*) from bgp_route_views b where b.cidr_block << p.network) as bgp_children from ip2city_dbiplite_probe_tbl p where masklen(p.network) between 16 and 22 and not exists (select 1 from bgp_route_views b where b.cidr_block << p.network) order by masklen(p.network), 1 limit 25"

Those are ranges appearing unitary in both sources. Then probe several /24s inside one and compare:

sudo -u cronuser env PGDATABASE=postgres /var/trugeo/check_geo_ip-api/bin/check_geo_ip-api -count 1 -country US -ipv4-only

That won't target a specific range, so the honest way to run this is a small purpose-built probe of chosen /24s. If cities or ZIPs differ across /24s within a range that both sources call unitary, your hypothesis is confirmed and decomposition must be driven by measurement rather than by BGP evidence alone — which would substantially expand apply_splits's remit. I can write that experiment as a disposable tool if you want it; it's maybe 30 lines and a few hundred API calls.
multiple_markets

Agreed, and I'd add: enforce it server-side, not only in the GUI. A GUI-only guard is bypassed by anyone using the API directly, which is exactly how an out-of-market spend incident would happen. So the API should reject multiple codes unless multiple_markets=1 is explicitly present, with the GUI toggle simply setting that parameter. Default off, refusal explicit.
EC2 for the frontend — more viable than it looks

There's a property of the current design that makes this work: expansion happens in Go, not in SQL. Only prefix rows cross the database connection. Indianapolis is 5,654 rows over the wire, from which the API generates 3,444,280 lines locally. So an API on EC2 talking to Postgres on Mint30 moves kilobytes per request, not tens of megabytes — the expensive part happens on the EC2 side, next to the client.

That said:

    Do not expose Postgres to the internet. WireGuard or an SSH tunnel between EC2 and Mint30, with Postgres still listening only on localhost or the tunnel interface.
    Mint30 becomes a single point of failure for a service on your production websites' infrastructure. Acceptable for internal use, not for anything customer-facing.
    Add authentication and rate limiting at the edge. The service has neither. One unauthenticated request can force millions of rows of enumeration, which is a trivial denial-of-service. You already run nginx or ALB for the other sites, so reuse that.
    The probe pipeline must stay with the database. It's DB-bound, not compute-bound, so splitting it from Postgres would be the wrong seam.

Given the AWS migration was already planned, and that the timezone change was anticipated for it, my inclination is to move Postgres and the API together rather than straddle. Running the frontend on EC2 first is a reasonable interim step precisely because the wire cost is low — but it's worth treating as interim rather than the destination.

And it refutes what I told you two messages ago

My first 8-sample run returned one ZIP, and I concluded ip-api "answers at block granularity rather than per address," presenting that as an argument for the landmark table. The eight-sample run wasn't imprecise, it was misleading, and I built an argument on it.

The tool now prints a sampling caveat whenever it hasn't enumerated every block, because only a SPLIT verdict is safe from a partial sample.
What this does to the plan

ZIP-level accuracy requires decomposing every range wider than /24, not only BGP-split ones. That's a real change to apply_splits, whose current trigger is BGP evidence. Worth sizing before committing to it:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select masklen(network) as len, count(*) as ranges, sum(2^(24-masklen(network)))::bigint as would_become_24s from ip2city_dbiplite_probe_tbl where masklen(network) < 24 group by 1 order by 1"

The would_become_24s total is the new row count, and each new row is a probe. Against your current 2,082,000-range backlog at 45/min, that is the deciding number — and it almost certainly makes ZIP targeting contingent on commercial ip-api rather than merely slow.

Landmarks remain valuable, but the reason changed. Not because ip-api is coarse — it isn't — but as independent ground truth to validate it. Your Hemet result shows ip-api producing a plausible ZIP distribution, yet nothing there proves the 13 blocks it assigned to 92543 are actually 92543. A landmark with a known address inside one of those blocks is what confirms or refutes it.

Next candidates should be eyeball ranges, chosen by origin ASN rather than by width, so you don't retest AWS:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select p.network, masklen(p.network) as len, p.city, p.state_code, (select string_agg(distinct b.origin_asn::text, ',') from bgp_route_views b where p.network <<= b.cidr_block) as origin_asns from ip2city_dbiplite_probe_tbl p where masklen(p.network) between 18 and 22 order by random() limit 30"

Cable and telco ASNs — Charter 20115, Comcast 7922, Cox 22773, AT&T 7018 — are the population that matters. Then:

/var/trugeo/probe_range_split/bin/probe_range_split -range 76.90.64.0/20 -samples 16

A /20 costs 16 calls, about 21 seconds. Ten ranges is 160 calls and gives you a defensible base rate for how often BGP-invisible ZIP splits occur — which is the number that decides whether the landmark table is a refinement or a prerequisite.

Evidence for the T-Mobile claim

The mechanism is documented at the standards level. RFC 6146 states that public IPv4 addresses assigned to a NAT64 translator are shared among several IPv6-only clients. Cisco's NAT64 documentation describes its purpose as letting an IPv6-only client reach an IPv4-only server. 464XLAT (RFC 6877) pairs that provider-side translator with a customer-side one that synthesises a local IPv4 address on the device so applications believe they have normal IPv4.

T-Mobile US specifically: a field report notes it won't hand out an IPv4 address on a dual APN in most markets, and an OpenWrt thread reports consumer lines being IPv6-only with CLAT supplying IPv4.

The geolocation consequence is independently attested, though only by secondary sources: mobile data exits through a handful of regional gateways, often hundreds of miles away, and under CGNAT the public IP maps to the carrier's infrastructure location rather than the subscriber's city. (Content rephrased for compliance with licensing restrictions.)

So: mechanism authoritative, T-Mobile behaviour well-corroborated, geolocation impact plausible but attested by commercial blogs rather than primary research. Which is exactly why measuring it yourself is better than trusting any of it — and your instinct to test every carrier is right.
The instrument

-asn N samples one /24 from each of an ASN's prefixes, spreading as widely across its footprint as the sample allows:

cd /home/boris/geo/src/claude && git pull origin main && ./geo/pipeline/deploy.sh
/var/trugeo/probe_range_split/bin/probe_range_split -asn 21928 -samples 40

Verdicts: NON GEOGRAPHIC (one city across every probe — translator signature), HIGHLY CONCENTRATED (few regional gateways), RESOLVABLE (varies by market). 40 probes is under a minute per carrier.

It deliberately reports a property of your data, not of the network — whether your sources can distinguish markets for that operator. That's the question that decides inclusion, and unlike subscriber truth it's directly measurable.

Find the ASNs from your own probe results rather than my recollection:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select p.\"as\", p.isp, count(*) as probed, count(distinct p.city) as cities from ip2city_dbiplite_probe_tbl p where p.ran_at is not null and p.likely_mobile_cgnat group by 1,2 order by 3 desc limit 25"

Then confirm each ASN has enough footprint to sample:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select origin_asn, count(*) as prefixes from bgp_route_views where family(cidr_block)=4 group by 1 having count(*) > 20 order by 2 desc limit 40"

On your existing carrier machinery

What you have is mobileISPKeywords plus the likely_mobile_cgnat column — a classifier, not an exclusion. Nothing in the pipeline acts on that flag: mobile ranges are probed and returned like any other. That's fortunate, because it means acting on a test result is a one-line filter rather than new infrastructure, and it can be scoped per-ASN rather than all-or-nothing.

The keyword list is also carefully built — Google Fi excluded so it can't catch Google Fiber, C Spire omitted because it sells both mobile and fixed under one name. Worth preserving that discipline if you extend it.
One asymmetry worth noting before you decide

Your reallocation argument against excluding corporate ranges doesn't transfer to carrier NAT pools, and I think that's the substantive difference. An AWS range might one day serve Google Fiber subscribers, so excluding it risks a future false negative. But a NAT64 translator pool will never become geographically meaningful — it is architecturally a shared egress point. Excluding it forgoes nothing that could later exist.

The cost of exclusion there is only the impressions themselves: a T-Mobile Home Internet subscriber streaming on a big screen is a real viewer at a real address, and AS21928 carries both the mobile and the fixed-wireless product. That's the trade to weigh, and the per-ASN measurement won't separate them — which may argue for testing at prefix level within AS21928 rather than treating the ASN as one population.

Your decomposition numbers

Summing your output: 368,520 ranges become 3,368,502 /24s — roughly 3.0M net new rows, taking the table from 2,089,296 to about 5.09M.

That is the whole ZIP question in one figure. At 57,600 probes/day a cycle goes from ~36 days to ~88 days. ZIP-level targeting is therefore not merely helped by commercial ip-api, it's gated on it.

Two things in that distribution stand out:

The /9 through /12 rows — 28 ranges producing 216,000 /24s. Almost certainly the cloud and backbone space from your earlier list. You've decided not to exclude them, which I agree with, but decomposing an Amazon /9 into 32,768 /24s and probing each to learn it's still a datacenter is 32,768 wasted calls. This is the case for deprioritising rather than excluding — probe them last. That preserves coverage while spending the constrained resource where it pays, and it needs a local sort column since I removed the ordering that used a correlated subquery.

The /16 row — 2,648 ranges producing 677,888 /24s, the single largest contributor at 20% of the total.
Something in that output I want to check

AS174 appears in every single row. Cogent is transit, not the origin of Comcast or AT&T customer space, so a containment match against a Cogent announcement in all 30 rows suggests bgp_route_views holds an unusually broad aggregate from them:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select cidr_block, masklen(cidr_block) as len, origin_asn, updated_at from bgp_route_views where origin_asn = 174 order by masklen(cidr_block) limit 10"

This matters beyond cosmetics. rebuild_probe_tbl.sql materialises excluded ASN prefixes by joining bgp_route_views on origin_asn, then excludes any range contained in them. If an excluded ASN ever announced an aggregate that broad, the exclusion would silently remove enormous amounts of space. Your DoD rules expanded to 8,189 prefixes, which looks bounded, but the mechanism is the same and worth verifying:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select x.origin_asn, min(masklen(b.cidr_block)) as widest, count(*) as prefixes from geo_exclusions x join bgp_route_views b on b.origin_asn = x.origin_asn where x.active and x.origin_asn is not null group by 1 order by 2 limit 10"

If widest is smaller than about 12 for any excluded ASN, that rule is removing more than intended and should be reviewed.

The Hemet experiment shows that ZIP-code boundary crossing is not sequential: any address in the 16 can land in a different one of the 3 ZIP codes, and in some cases, a /24 probably can as well (example from other countries: Baarle Nassau and Baarle Hertog). It is just an inaccuracy that is part of ZIP-code targeting. Landmarks will not reduce these minor deviations into adjacent ZIP codes.

The 0.0.0.0/0 row is a latent trap, not a cosmetic one

rebuild_probe_tbl.sql materialises every ASN-excluded operator's prefixes and removes any range contained in them. Had an ASN announcing a default route ever been added to geo_exclusions, that one row would have excluded the entire address space — emptying the probe table with no error and nothing pointing at the cause.

Your exclusions are safe today: widest is /8 from AS749 and AS721, correct since IANA designated whole /8s to DoD. But the mechanism was one row away from a silent catastrophe.

prefixRange now rejects zero-length prefixes, and the rebuild refuses to run if any ASN exclusion expands wider than /8. Delete the existing row:

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "delete from bgp_route_views where masklen(cidr_block) = 0 returning cidr_block, origin_asn"

The finding that actually matters for ZIP targeting

Look at Comcast's ZIPs: 10123 sixteen times, 07175 eight times, 60666, 98111, 02112, 99209, 30302. Those are not residential delivery areas — they're PO Box and unique ZIPs. 10123 is the Empire State Building. 60666 is O'Hare's mail facility. These are city-centroid placeholders, returned when the provider knows the city but not the ZIP.

Contrast Hemet: 92543, 92544, 92545 — real residential ZIPs, correctly distributed.

So ip-api's ZIP quality is bimodal: genuinely per-block in some ranges, a city placeholder in others. A ZIP list built from this would target the Empire State Building for a large slice of Comcast's New York footprint. That's the strongest argument yet for your landmark table — not for boundary precision, where you're right that landmarks won't help, but for detecting which ZIPs are placeholders. A cheap first pass is flagging ZIPs that are PO-Box-only in USPS data.

Also worth noting: four Comcast-announced 48.4x blocks returned ISP "AviationAI" with ZIP 10013. 48.0.0.0/8 is recently-allocated space, and ip-api evidently carries stale attribution for it. Newly-allocated ranges are a distinct data-quality risk.
Your decomposition rule — one design question before I build it

I want to name a property that makes your rule safer than it first appears: a decomposition exclusion is not a targeting exclusion. The range stays in the table with its coarse city, it merely isn't split into /24s. So a wrong match costs granularity, never coverage — no false negatives. That makes the rule much safer than the DoD-style exclusions, and it's why I think it should live in a separate table rather than in geo_exclusions: mixing them invites someone applying a decomposition rule as a targeting filter.

The design question is how to obtain the registrant. Per-range RDAP means ~368,520 lookups against RIR rate limits. But every decomposition candidate has an origin ASN from BGP, and ASN-to-organisation is a far smaller mapping — and you already have it partly populated, because probe_tbl."as" holds strings like AS16509 Amazon.com, Inc. from ip-api. So: bootstrap an ASN-to-org table from existing probe results, fill gaps by RDAP per ASN rather than per range, and match the exclusion patterns against that.

Two things to confirm:

    Match on ASN organisation rather than per-range registrant? Far cheaper, and correct wherever an operator's ASN is dedicated. It's wrong where an ISP announces a customer's assignment under its own ASN — but that case is exactly the one you want decomposed anyway.
    Pattern matching, since registrant strings vary — Amazon.com, Inc. versus Amazon Technologies Inc. versus Amazon Data Services NoVa. I'd use ILIKE patterns with the reason recorded per row, and Google explicitly absent per your instruction.

"decomposition exclusion": name and separate handling from geo_exclusions approved.

Use ip-api, not rdap-lookup, to determine the registrant. Probing is not occurring while decomposition runs (confirm). Run a counter to avoid exceeding the 45/h limit.

Do not match decomposition exclusion on ASN. We must not oversweep the exclusion. Doing so by operator name (which can be matched using the like keyword) ensures that additions, drops and ownership changes from numberspace holdingsare processed correctly. Doing it by ASNs doesn't.

Probe each /28 in T-Mobile's /24 ranges. This will tell us whether T-Mobile is resolvable to ZIP-code level or only to DMA.

Thought (7)

No — probing is not excluded during decomposition. The locks say so:
script	own lock	mutation (fd7)	probe (fd8)
daily_pipeline.sh	yes	yes	no
probe_batch.sh	yes	no	—
monthly_dbip.sh	yes	yes	yes, blocking

monthly_dbip excludes probing; daily_pipeline does not. And they overlap in practice: daily_pipeline runs 02:00–02:17 while the 02:05 probe batch starts inside that window. So a registrant lookup during decomposition would collide with probe_batch for the same 45/min budget and produce exactly the 429 storm you just saw from my back-to-back runs.

The fix follows the pattern monthly_dbip already uses — take_lock_blocking "$PROBE_LOCK" — but scoped to the lookup step only, so the whole nightly pipeline doesn't queue behind a 53-minute batch.

Also flagging: you wrote 45/h; the limit throughout this project is 45/min. I've built to 45/min with a flag.

decomposition_exclusions.sql

Merged as 837fc6b.
Answering your points

Probing is not excluded during decomposition — confirmed negative. daily_pipeline takes its own lock and the mutation lock, but never the probe lock. monthly_dbip does take it, blocking. So a registrant lookup inside decomposition would contend with probe_batch for the same 45/min. The fix is take_lock_blocking "$PROBE_LOCK" around the lookup step only — the pattern already exists in monthly_dbip, and scoping it narrowly avoids queueing the whole nightly run behind a 53-minute batch.

Operator name, not ASN — your reasoning is better than mine. I'd proposed ASN because it was cheap; you're right that it oversweeps and, worse, keeps oversweeping after ownership changes. The name follows the range. Implemented as ILIKE patterns, no ASN matching anywhere.

ip-api, not RDAP — and this makes the lookup nearly free. isp and org are already stored on every probed row. So for a probed range the check costs zero calls. The consequence is a sequencing rule I've made explicit: a range with no probe has no registrant, so it is deferred rather than decomposed. Decomposing before the registrant is known would defeat the rule entirely. That also removes most of the rate-limit problem — the counter matters only if you want to probe wide ranges ahead of their turn.

On the safety asymmetry, which is why I kept the tables separate as you approved: geo_exclusions removes a range from probing and output, so a wrong entry is an invisible false negative. decomposition_exclusions only stops decomposition — the range stays targetable at its original width. A wrong entry costs granularity, never coverage. That means this table can be populated far more freely than the DoD one.

Seeded with Amazon only. Hosting and colocation candidates are listed but commented out, unverified against your database — the project's rule is never to exclude on a guess. Google is explicitly absent with the reason recorded in the file, as are the backbones.

I agree with the probing fix.

ZIP codes for geotargeting as a stand-in for socioeconomic/demographic/psychographic cohorts is the responsibility of the media buying agency. This is done using Claritas PRIZM, Census Bureau data, or similar. None of these sources would include ZIP codes of post-office box installations, airports, etc. So T-Mobile customers watching on its network (rather than WiFi from another source, the dominant connection at home) would become effectively unavailable, as would fixed-4G/5G customers, but they would be available to local or backfill advertisers buying entire DMAs. Not a disaster, although it may become one if 6G is more competitive with wired Internet service.

On the probing fix

Implemented, but deliberately inert: DECOMPOSE_LOOKUP_REGISTRANT defaults to 0. Taking the probe lock unconditionally would cost a skipped hourly batch — about 2,400 probes — every night the pipeline is still running at 02:05, in exchange for nothing until the registrant lookup exists. Setting it to 1 is what serialises ip-api across the whole pipeline. Verified: default takes no lock; with the lock held elsewhere the blocking acquisition waits and alerts rather than failing; an invalid value exits 2.
Still unbuilt, so nothing enforces it yet

apply_splits does not consult decomposition_exclusions. The table, the ILIKE matching, the defer-when-unprobed rule and the lock plumbing all exist and are individually testable, but the decomposer is untouched. That plus decomposing all sub-/24 ranges rather than only BGP-split ones is the next piece of work, and they should land together since the exclusion table is what stops those 3,368,502 rows being inflated by datacentre space.

sudo -u cronuser psql -d postgres -c "select tablename, indexname from pg_indexes where tablename in ('ip2city_dbiplite_probe_tbl','dma2city_tbl') order by 1,2"

Then see the operator check work on your real data — dry run, writes nothing:

sudo -u cronuser env PGDATABASE=postgres /var/trugeo/apply_splits/bin/apply_splits -dry-run -ensure-source-column=false

Read the two new log lines: registrant: N excluded by operator, M deferred with no probe, followed by the operators ranked by /24 rows avoided.
What the decomposition change does

Two checks, both default on, independently disableable:

    Operator check — refuses a range whose ip-api isp/org matches an active decomposition_exclusions pattern, by name with ILIKE, never by ASN.
    Defer rule — skips a range never probed, since it has no registrant and decomposing would bypass the exclusion. It becomes eligible once probed. This is the unavoidable consequence of sourcing the registrant from ip-api rather than RDAP.

A missing table is fatal, naming both the file to run and the -operator-check=false bypass. Silently reverting would decompose datacentre space and spend probe budget on it, which is the thing being prevented.

Verified on PostgreSQL 15 across all four branches: one Charter range decomposes, Amazon is operator-excluded, the unprobed range defers, the prefix-excluded one is still caught by geo_exclusions. Each flag off returns exactly the expected range.
The defer rule has a consequence worth naming now

Your own numbers make this concrete. Section 4 of the exclusions file showed nearly every wide range as defer, registrant unknown — and section 5 lists only 30 operators, because only probed ranges have a registrant at all. With 18,334 of 2,089,296 probed, the vast majority of the 368,520 sub-/24 ranges will defer.

So decomposition is now gated on probe coverage, and progresses as the cycle progresses. That's correct rather than a defect — decomposing before the registrant is known is exactly what you told me not to do — but it means the full 3.37M-row decomposition is a consequence of completing a probe cycle, not something that can be run ahead of it.

HP Inc. at 4,224 rows from two ranges is the current top of that list, ahead of Amazon at 2,148. Worth a look: HP has no consumer access product, so it's a candidate for the exclusions file on the same reasoning as Amazon — but unlike Amazon you haven't named it, so I've left it alone.

Still not built: decomposing all sub-/24 ranges rather than only dbip_split_candidates. That needs no Go change — -candidates accepts any table or view with a network column, so a view over ip2city_dbiplite_tbl where masklen < 24 and source = 'dbip' would do it. I haven't created that view, since turning it on multiplies the probe backlog and should be a deliberate act.

On your point about ZIP-level availability

Your framing is right and it changes what we should build, not just what we should tolerate. PRIZM and Census tract data have no notion of a PO-Box ZIP or an airport ZIP, so a T-Mobile subscriber whose ip-api ZIP resolves to one of those is not merely imprecise — that subscriber is unbuyable at ZIP level, because the buy-side list will never contain that ZIP. The correct treatment is therefore not to exclude the carrier and not to emit the bad ZIP either: the range stays in the DMA-level output, where it is genuinely correct, and is withheld from ZIP-level output. That is a per-output-tier decision, which is why decomposition_exclusions being separate from geo_exclusions keeps paying off — neither table expresses "valid at DMA, invalid at ZIP," and we will need a third, narrower thing for that.

The 6G caveat you raise is the real risk, and it is a data risk rather than an architecture one: if mobile becomes the dominant home connection, the share of our audience that is DMA-only grows, and the ZIP tier silently covers less of the market without any error appearing anywhere. That argues for reporting ZIP-tier coverage as a measured percentage of DMA-tier reach, so the erosion is visible when it starts.

Thought (13) + Tools (3)

Three findings, one of which contradicts an earlier measurement and matters more than the rest.
1. The dry run is vacuous — the registrant gate was never reached

Your numbers add up exactly: 82 already /24 or narrower + 260 excluded by prefix = 342, the whole candidate set. Both of those tests run before the registrant tests in the loop, so 0 excluded by operator, 0 deferred does not mean the new logic found nothing — it means nothing ever arrived at it. Thought (8)

PR #34 is up. Answers to each of your questions, several of which needed correcting.
1. RDAP versus ip-api — your assumption was wrong, and that is what was breaking decomposition

The two do not carry the same field, and they cannot be used at the same point in the workflow. That second part is the operative difference and it is the one you intuited.

RDAP is RIR registration data: the organisation an allocation is registered to, plus reassignment records beneath it. It is keyed on the prefix, so it answers for any range at any time.

ip-api isp/org are derived commercial descriptions of who appears to be operating an address. They are inconsistently populated — that is why the code had to coalesce isp then org — and they exist only as a side effect of probing one address in the range.

So under ip-api, an unprobed range has no registrant and must be deferred. That is not theoretical. Verified on a real database against live ARIN, an Amazon /16 that has never been probed:
registrant source	outcome
rdap	1 excluded by operator — Amazon Data Services Northern Virginia matched %amazon%
ip-api	0 excluded by operator, 2 deferred — the exclusion silently did not apply

RDAP is now the default. Your existing %amazon% seed works unchanged because ARIN's name contains "Amazon", but note RDAP names differ from ip-api names — ARIN says Amazon Data Services Northern Virginia where ip-api says Amazon.com, so %aws% will never match an RDAP name.

The other win is cost. One RDAP answer describes the whole containing allocation, not the prefix asked about:

    query 54.144.0.0/16 → allocation 54.144.0.0 – 54.147.255.255
    query 76.90.64.0/20 → allocation 76.80.0.0 – 76.95.255.255 (Charter Communications Inc, a /12)

So the cache is keyed on the returned allocation. That is what makes 371,757 candidates affordable, and it draws on a different budget from ip-api entirely.
2. Why your apply_splits run found nothing — and it is worse than the exclusion logic

Your diagnostics show the real problem, and it is not the registrant gate.

dbip_split_candidates holds 396 rows, rebuilt in a single pass at 02:22 on 13 Sep. Of the 260 killed by prefix exclusion, essentially all are DoD: 214/8, 55/8, 6/8, 215/8, 11/8, 21/8, 22/8, 28/8, 29/8, 7/8, plus 132.80/12 and 132.128/12. Meanwhile 371,757 sub-/24 db-ip ranges are not candidates at all.

check_range_splits only flags ranges with more specific BGP children. Only 396 currently qualify. So decomposition as wired addresses roughly 0.1% of the problem, and most of that 0.1% is space you already exclude. The 371,757 — including the 2.0.0.0/16 Austin and 4.x/16 Monroe rows from your earlier query — have no BGP children and are therefore invisible to it, yet a /16 attributed to one city is precisely the error decomposition exists to fix.

The view you called optional is not optional. It is the only route to the actual opportunity, and it needs no Go change — rdap_registrant -fill already defaults to that full set rather than to dbip_split_candidates.
3. -repeat, exactly how it works

A new table probe_stability_tbl, one row per (cohort, address, round): network, probe_ip, round, observed_at, status, country_code, city, state_code, zip, isp, org, mobile_ipapi, err.

The addresses are fixed for the life of the cohort. This is the whole design. If each round re-randomised the address inside the block, a changed city could mean either the block moved or two hosts inside it sit in different places, and nothing afterwards could separate those. Holding probe_ip constant makes any change unambiguously drift.

Re-using a -cohort label reloads its original addresses and continues the round numbering, so rounds can be days apart across separate invocations — no long-lived process. Failed probes are stored with err populated, because a round that dropped its failures would make a cohort look more stable than it is.

The report gives: addresses tracked, rounds per address, percentage whose city moved, percentage whose ZIP moved, and the fastest interval over which any change was observed. That last number is the one that answers your acceptability question — it says how long an answer stays true.

City and ZIP churn are reported separately on purpose: the DMA tier resolves through city and survives ZIP churn, the ZIP tier does not.
4. Your daily-cycle assumption does not survive the arithmetic

I measured the limit rather than arguing about it. A single live ip-api call returns:

X-Rl: 44 calls remaining in the current window
X-Ttl: 60 seconds until the window resets

The 45/min limit is real, enforced per source IP, and readable from headers. That is 64,800 calls/day. Against a 2,070,962-range backlog that is 32 days. A one-day cycle needs 1,438/min, 32× the limit.

So "a full probing cycle will be completed in a day or less" is not reachable by finding headroom — it needs the paid batch endpoint, for which scaffolding already exists in check_geo_ip-api but is deliberately unimplemented pending the verified request format. Your other project seeing no errors above 45/min is worth understanding, but X-Rl counting down on our own IP right now is direct evidence that the budget applies to us.

check_geo_ip-api now logs its X-Rl low water mark, so the live cycle characterises the limit continuously at zero extra cost. ipapi_rate_test is built for the 1000-address run, defaults to stopping at the first 429, and draws only from already probed ranges so it never touches the backlog.

One thing to know before running it: probe_batch uses 2400 of the 2700 calls available per hour, leaving about 300. A 1000-call test needs 22 minutes of exclusive budget and cannot fit. Run it from a different source IP if you have one, because a block would halt the pipeline and we cannot lift it on demand.
5. likely_mobile_cgnat — confirmed, with a correction

It was already being set on every ip-api probe. But not from ip-api's mobile field — from a keyword match on isp/org (wireless, cellular, mobile, mobility, pcs, sprint, metropcs, boost). mobile is not in ip-api's default field set and was never requested, so the mobile=false you saw in earlier output was our keyword verdict wearing the name of a source field.

Both are now used, and the flag is their union, biased to over-mark: a false negative publishes a ZIP no demographic cohort contains, a false positive only demotes a range to DMA level. Disagreements are logged rather than resolved silently.

This also shrinks the Sprint concern I raised last turn — sprint is already in the keyword list, so 167.20.43.0/24 returning Sprint Communications is correctly flagged mobile. It matters for decomposition_exclusions patterns, not for the ZIP gate.

The keyword list now exists in two tools and should move to a table. I have not done that; flagging it rather than expanding this change.
6. Puerto Rico — ip-api returns neither 'PR' as a region nor a ZIP

Settled by direct query:

{"country":"Puerto Rico","countryCode":"PR","region":"","regionName":"Cabo Rojo",
 "city":"Puerto Real","zip":"","isp":"T-Mobile USA, Inc.","mobile":true}

So: countryCode is PR, not US — ip-api treats Puerto Rico as a separate country. region is empty, regionName is the municipio, and zip is empty.

That explains why your null-state query returned zero rows: the pipeline filters -country US, so PR ranges are never selected for probing and no PR rows exist in the probe table at all. Admitting them would need the country filter widened, and they would still arrive with an empty state_code, so the dma2city_tbl join could not resolve — and you have confirmed there is no DMA for PR regardless.

(My attempt at a contrasting PR address was wrong — 24.51.0.1 is Nvidia in Santa Clara. The first result is definitive on its own.)

That queries nothing. It reports how many candidates the empty cache cannot answer, which on your data should be a number near 371,757. Then 200 real queries, at the deliberately slow 1/sec default:

sudo -u cronuser env PGDATABASE=postgres /var/trugeo/rdap_registrant/bin/rdap_registrant -fill -limit 200

Watch the covers= figure on each line. That is the payoff to measure: Charter's 76.90.64.0/20 resolved to a 76.80.0.0–76.95.255.255 allocation, one query covering a /12. If the average covers= is large, the 371,757 collapse into a few thousand queries. If it is small, RDAP costs more than I have estimated and we should know that before scheduling it.

Re-run the dry run afterwards to see how much 200 queries actually bought:

sudo -u cronuser env PGDATABASE=postgres /var/trugeo/rdap_registrant/bin/rdap_registrant -fill -dry-run
sudo -u cronuser env PGDATABASE=postgres /var/trugeo/apply_splits/bin/apply_splits -dry-run -ensure-source-column=false

The apply_splits run should now report a nonzero registrant: line for the first time — that gate has never actually executed on your data.

If you would rather have the two SQL files pasted into the shell than pull them, say so and I will emit them as heredocs; both are verified free of mid-line # and backslashes, so they survive your paste path intact. But git is the route you set for this project and the branch already has them.

Merged as 9ff29ca. Two faults, both surfaced by that run — one was mine.
What went wrong

The permission error. Both new tables use bigserial, and a bigserial needs USAGE on its sequence as well as the table grant. I gave neither. It fails per row rather than at connect time, which is why it looked like a tool bug. Both SQL files now grant to cronuser inside a DO block that checks pg_roles first.

The wasted RDAP budget — my design error. Look at what it was querying: 7.0.0.0/8, 21.0.0.0/8, 22.0.0.0/8, 29.0.0.0/8, 30.0.0.0/8, 214.128.0.0/9. That is DoD space. apply_splits discards prefix-excluded ranges before it ever consults the registrant, so a registrant for those can never change any decision. I sorted candidates widest-first to maximise coverage per query, which is correct, but the widest ranges in your candidate set are exactly the permanently excluded ones. Every one of those 43 calls bought an unusable answer.

loadCandidates now filters geo_exclusions in SQL, served by your existing gist index. Verified: 7 db-ip rows against 5 active DoD prefixes yields 2 candidates.

One correction to my own reporting. The dry run said 372015 queried. That number is an upper bound, not a forecast — each real query returns an allocation covering many later candidates, and a dry run cannot know boundaries it declined to fetch. It now says so rather than implying 372,015 calls are needed.

Thought (19) + Tools (1)

RDAP is cheap, and the registrant data is more interesting than the cost measurement.
Coverage: the design works

25 queries returned allocations covering roughly 109.8 million addresses — an average of 4.4M per query. Better, during a 35-candidate walk, 10 were answered free from allocations fetched earlier in the same run. That 28.6% hit rate is the compounding effect, and it should climb steeply as the walk descends from /9s into the /20–/23 band where 350,000+ of your candidates live, because those cluster densely inside single allocations.

I will not extrapolate a total from 25 queries at the widest end, where candidates are sparsest and coverage is worst. Run -limit 500 and the already covered versus queried ratio becomes a real measurement.

One incidental confirmation: 8.96.0.0/11 resolved to 8.8.9.0 – 8.127.255.255. That starts mid-block because 8.8.8.0/24 is carved out for Google DNS. It is not a CIDR at all, which is exactly why the cache stores start_ip/end_ip rather than a cidr column. That decision was speculative when I made it; it is now load-bearing.
What the registrants actually show

This is the finding. Your coarse-range backlog is dominated by legacy corporate /8s and /12s, and now they have names:
registrant	candidate	/24s it would generate
Ford Motor Company	19.128.0.0/9	32,768
T-Mobile USA	100.128.0.0/9	32,768
JPMorgan Chase	169.64.0.0/10, 169.16.0.0/12	20,480
Prudential Insurance	48.96/11, 48.16/12, 48.48/12	16,384
CoreWeave	48.128/11, 48.80/12	12,288

HP Inc., Apple, Bank of America, Texas DIR, USDA	five /12s	20,480

Those 25 candidates alone would generate 182,272 /24 rows. At 45 calls a minute that is 2.8 days of your entire probe budget — from 25 ranges out of 371,289.

Broken down by what the registrant actually is:

corp       81,920 /24s   44.9%   1.3 probe-days
eyeball    45,056 /24s   24.7%   0.7 probe-days
cloud      30,720 /24s   16.9%   0.5 probe-days
backbone   12,288 /24s    6.7%   0.2 probe-days
gov         8,192 /24s    4.5%   0.1 probe-days
dod         4,096 /24s    2.2%   0.1 probe-days

68.5% of the cost goes to registrants with no consumer access product. Ford, Prudential, JPMorgan, Bank of America, HP, Apple, Texas Department of Information Resources, USDA. Only 24.7% reaches T-Mobile, Comcast and Verizon — the networks the exercise exists to reach.
This resolves your reluctance, using your own reasoning

You said you were loathe to exclude corporate ranges because reallocation from Amazon, or Ford, is imaginable in a way it is not from DoD. That objection was correct against an ASN rule, and it is why you directed name matching instead. But it dissolves against an RDAP registrant rule, for exactly the reason you gave for preferring names:

If Ford sells 19.0.0.0/8 to an ISP tomorrow, the ARIN registrant changes. The pattern stops matching. The range decomposes on the next run, automatically, with no list to maintain. The exclusion is self-healing on ownership change — which is precisely the property you wanted from name matching over ASN matching.

And the downside remains bounded: a decomposition exclusion costs granularity, never coverage. 19.0.0.0/8 stays in the probe table and stays targetable at its original width. If Ford ever does serve eyeballs from it, it is reachable the whole time, just coarsely.

I have not inserted anything. The named candidates on this evidence would be Ford, Prudential, JPMorgan, Bank of America, HP, Apple, Texas DIR, USDA, CoreWeave — and Microsoft, which you previously left open. Level 3 stays out, as you directed, because backbones carry customer assignments; this run confirms 4.0.0.0/8 is Level 3 Parent, which is the Monroe LA artefact.
A gap in geo_exclusions

148.16.0.0/12 resolved to DoD Network Information Center, allocation 148.10.0.0 – 148.50.255.255. It survived the prefix filter, so it is not in geo_exclusions. Your DoD seeding covered the /8s but not this. Worth checking how much more DoD space is in the same position:

sudo -u cronuser env PGDATABASE=postgres psql -d postgres -c "select r.registrant, count(*) as allocations, sum((r.end_ip - r.start_ip)+1) as addresses from rdap_registrant_tbl r where r.registrant ilike '%dod%' or r.registrant ilike '%defense%' or r.registrant ilike '%defence%' or r.registrant ilike '%army%' or r.registrant ilike '%navy%' or r.registrant ilike '%air force%' group by 1 order by 3 desc"

Warm 500 more, which is the measurement that settles the cost question:

sudo -u cronuser env PGDATABASE=postgres /var/trugeo/rdap_registrant/bin/rdap_registrant -fill -limit 500

That is about 8.5 minutes at 1/sec. Read the final line: N already covered by cache, 500 queried. If N is well above 500, coverage is winning and the whole set is affordable.

Then the ranked cost-by-registrant table, which is section 3 of the SQL file and the right basis for any exclusion decision:

sudo -u cronuser env PGDATABASE=postgres psql -d postgres -c "select cov.registrant, count(*) as wide_ranges, sum(2 ^ (24 - masklen(d.network)))::bigint as sub24_rows, round(sum(2 ^ (24 - masklen(d.network)))/64800.0, 2) as probe_days, min(masklen(d.network)) as widest from ip2city_dbiplite_tbl d join lateral (select r.registrant from rdap_registrant_tbl r where r.start_ip <= host(network(d.network))::inet and r.end_ip >= host(broadcast(d.network))::inet order by (r.end_ip - r.start_ip) limit 1) cov on true where d.source = 'dbip' and family(d.network) = 4 and masklen(d.network) < 24 group by 1 order by sub24_rows desc limit 30"

That gives you probe-days per registrant against the current cache. Send it and we can decide the exclusion list on numbers rather than on my categorisation of who sells broadband.

Confirmed and corrected. Merged as 8d59f4d.
Direct answer: it was not so

decomposition_exclusions held four active Amazon patterns — %amazon%, %aws%, %amazon technologies%, %amazon data services%. They are now deactivated, and the policy file is self-enforcing: re-running it deactivates anything not on the DoD list, so the table converges on policy regardless of hand edits. Rows are deactivated rather than deleted so the history of what was once excluded stays readable.

Your reasoning is right and my earlier reasoning was wrong in a way the data now makes obvious. RDAP returns the registrant of an allocation. It cannot say whether a range inside that allocation serves infrastructure or end users. Your own run is the proof — it returned University of Michigan, Michigan State, Stanford, MIT, Grand Valley State, Merit Network, Utah Education Network, and the Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia. Universities run student housing. Those are residential eyeballs sitting behind a name that looks purely institutional. And the same applies to Ford, Boeing, Procter and Gamble, Eli Lilly: people at work consume media and are targets under your rules.

So the test is not "does this organisation sell broadband" but "can this space be ruled out as serving end users with certainty". Only DoD passes, and it passes for a reason unrelated to commerce: its space is not offered to the public at all.
The six DoD patterns, all observed rather than guessed

Every name appeared in your 500-query run. Three would be missed by the obvious patterns — Headquarters, USAISC contains no "army"; DIA contains no "defense"; Air Force Systems Networking contains no "DoD".

DIA is matched exactly, with no wildcards, because %dia% would also hit India, Media, Nvidia and Acadia. Verified: it excludes all six DoD names and leaves Nvidia Corporation and India Internet Media untouched.

Expect 8d59f4d. The file prints the enforcement result — the four Amazon rows should show active = f and the six DoD rows active = t. It then prints four reports:

    Section 3 lists every registrant in your cache and whether a pattern matches it. Read the unmatched rows for anything military; that is how more DoD spellings get found rather than guessed.
    Section 4 is the one I would act on. Your run found 148.16.0.0/12, 140.56.0.0/13, 157.216.0.0/13, 136.188.0.0/14 and many /15s all resolving to DoD registrants while passing the prefix filter — meaning they are not in geo_exclusions. Adding them there removes them from probing and output entirely, which is what DoD warrants but is a coverage-removing decision, so it is a report and not an action.
    Section 5 audits the other direction: active geo_exclusions prefixes whose registrant is not DoD. Under your policy those either have a reason worth re-reading or are a DoD spelling missing from section 1.
    Section 6 ranks decomposition cost per registrant in probe days.

The cost this policy commits to, stated plainly

Excluding only DoD means decomposition eventually generates about 3,368,502 sub-/24 rows. At the measured 64,800 calls a day that is roughly 52 days for the new rows and 84 days including the existing backlog.

That is the honest consequence, and I think it is the right trade — but it means exclusions were never the lever that makes decomposition affordable. The paid batch endpoint is. The scaffolding for it already exists in check_geo_ip-api, deliberately unimplemented pending the verified request format. If you want a daily cycle, that is the next thing to build, and it needs either the paid API documentation or a test account to verify the format against.

The policy is correct — six DoD patterns active, four Amazon patterns inactive. But your output surfaced three real bugs, and I've fixed them. Merged as ddd11ff.
The registrant data is partly wrong

MNT-ADSI with 26 allocations, APPLE-MNT, MICROSOFT-MAINT, ORCL-MNT, OPENDNS-MNT — those are not registrants. They are maintainer objects. Verified against live RIPE for 51.180.0.0 – 51.181.255.255, three entities carry the registrant role:
handle	formatted name	what it is
MNT-ADSI	MNT-ADSI	a maintainer
ORG-ARI3-RIPE	A100 ROW Inc	the actual holder
RIPE-NCC-HM-MNT	RIPE-NCC-HM-MNT	RIPE's hostmaster maintainer

I took the first in document order. The discriminator that generalises is that a maintainer's formatted name equals its handle, whereas a real organisation has a human name distinct from it. Fixed and verified: MNT-ADSI now returns A100 ROW Inc, APPLE-MNT returns Apple Inc.
RIPE-NCC-MANAGED-ADDRESS-BLOCK was suppressing 33.5 million addresses

ARIN answers 303 for early-registration space and redirects to the responsible registry. For 151.220.0.1 that lands on RIPE, which returns the entire 151.0.0.0/8 as RIPE-NCC-MANAGED-ADDRESS-BLOCK with no entities at all. I stored that as a 16.7M-address allocation with administrative filler as the registrant.

That is worse than storing nothing, because the coverage test then treats every candidate inside the block as answered and never queries it again. Two such rows — 151.0.0.0/8 and 46.0.0.0/8 — meant ~33.5 million addresses of your candidate set would never get a real registrant.

Placeholders now store a NULL registrant with a placeholder: note, and apply_splits treats that as known rather than unknown: the registry was asked and holds no assignment, which is positive evidence no DoD registration exists. Treating it as unknown would have deferred that space permanently, since no later query can improve the answer.
Section 6 never ran on your database

It aborted with function round(double precision, integer) does not exist — 2 ^ int returns double precision in PostgreSQL. That is why you never saw the probe-days table. Fixed. I also reordered the registrant report so matched rows come first; the old ordering with LIMIT 60 hid every DoD match, which is exactly what you saw.

Yes, the signal is genuinely ip-api's — X-Rl and X-Ttl come straight from 208.95.112.1, no CDN, no proxy, no Server header. But I tested the larger limits from this sandbox's IP rather than yours, and the answer is that there is nothing to take.
Roughly 420 calls. Not one returned 429.
offered/min	ok	stalls	effective/min
~2000 burst	57/60	3, including 45s of total silence	74, then stalled
180	99/120	21 (18%)	27.9
90	103/120	17 (14%)	28.1
45, contaminated	54/60	6 (10%)	26.2
45, after 10 min idle	58/60	2 (3%)	34.9

Control over the same window: example.com 40/40, rdap.arin.net 20/20, zero timeouts. So the stalls belong to ip-api, not to sandbox networking — I checked that specifically because my first 45/min run looked worse than 60/min and I did not trust it.

Offering more delivers less. ip-api throttles by stopping answering, not by refusing. A stall costs wall-clock time, so 90/min and 180/min both delivered about 28/min — worse than politely pacing at 45. Pushing 4× the documented rate bought nothing.
Two things this corrects

The 429 handler in check_geo_ip-api was dead code. A stall arrives as a transport error, so a throttled run recorded every affected range as status='error' and kept calling at full rate, deepening the throttling. It now treats a timeout or severed connection as a throttle signal and backs off, which is what the 429 branch was always meant to do. No data was lost — those ranges stay city IS NULL and get retried — but throughput was silently degrading with no diagnostic.

I overstated X-Rl earlier. I read X-Rl: 44 as a single per-IP quota. It is not. It moves non-monotonically — 43, 44, 42, 43, 42, 41 — and X-Ttl appeared in at least three distinct phases inside one burst (44, 59/60, 14). That is several independent backends behind one address, each with its own counter, not one budget draining. It cannot be read as remaining quota.
One finding you should treat as a hard rule

The penalty appears to persist. My 45/min run immediately after the 180/min abuse stalled 10% of the time; after ten minutes idle, 3%. That is two samples, so an indication rather than a measurement — but it is reason enough never to probe the ceiling from the IP your pipeline runs on. If you want to retest, do it from a different host.

Where this leaves the throughput problem

45/min is the practical ceiling and it is 64,800 calls a day. Against your 2,070,962 backlog that is 32 days, and against the 3,368,502 rows full decomposition would add it is another 52. No rate tuning changes that.

The only lever left is the paid batch endpoint, which takes many addresses per request and lifts the limit outright. The scaffolding is already in check_geo_ip-api — readIPBatch and parseBatchResponse — deliberately unimplemented because the request and response formats are unconfirmed. If you want a cycle measured in days rather than months, that is the next build, and it needs either the paid API documentation or a test key to verify the format against rather than guess it.
