What I built

geo/main.go gains -source. Default ranges is the old behaviour byte for byte. landmarks traces each distinct ovt_places_usa.ip_address with onpremises = true into a new address-keyed table. Classification is shared code, so landmark hops and range hops are classified identically by construction.

Four things could not be reused from the range path. Retries re-trace the same address, because the landmark address is the datum and the sampling helper would have recorded it in tried and failed attempt two with "range exhausted", silently capping every landmark at one try. Output is keyed on the address, because the existing table is ON CONFLICT (network) and many landmarks share a prefix, so each would overwrite the last and leave one arbitrary survivor — failing without raising anything. Targets are DISTINCT addresses, which is what takes the pass from ~1.2M traces to ~123k. And -pause-file stops the feeder rather than the workers, so in-flight traces finish.

geo/landmark_carrier_node.sql fills ip_address_range, ip_last_carrier_node and ip_last_carrier_node_range — three inet columns unpopulated since the table was created — by containment, with no traffic. Then it measures the fan-out distribution, by router IP and by hostname separately, and refuses to assign through a node above the bound. I did not pick the bound: it is a one-place CTE value set to 1, which is not a measurement but the only value unambiguous by construction, to be revised from the histogram.
On the BGP half, which I think needs your confirmation

I read "the db-ip | BGP RouteViews table" as ip2city_dbiplite_tbl, which carries both source='dbip' and source='routeviews' rows. On that reading the range half of the method is that table, and geo/main.go already traces it.

If you meant reading a carrier node out of BGP attributes, it cannot work. bgp_route_views.as_path is NULL for every production row, because the ingester runs without -per-peer. More to the point, even with paths the second-to-last ASN is a whole company — AS7018 is AT&T in fifty states, so "landmark and subscriber share an upstream AS" is true for millions of addresses and says nothing about a ZIP. The geography is in the node's reverse DNS, where lightspeed.btrgla.sbcglobal.net names a metro, and BGP has no equivalent. So section 6 reports AS agreement as an attribute, never as a reason to assign.

Rather than commit 18 days, I'd suggest measuring yield per probe on two or three metros first. Say if you want me to build that restriction.

Thought (22)

Very informative run. Three defects in it, one of which breaks the method. Let me answer your question first, then show the evidence.
The AT&T point was me answering a question you didn't ask

You meant mtr on the probe range's random IP. That's what geo/main.go already does, so there was nothing to clarify and I should have just said so.

What I was arguing against was a different thing: deriving the node from BGP attributes instead of from a traceroute. The finest-grained thing BGP gives you is an AS number, and an AS number names a company, not a router. AS7018 is all of AT&T, in every state. So "landmark and subscriber are behind the same AS" is true for tens of millions of addresses and cannot narrow anything to a ZIP, whereas an mtr hostname like po-1-rur202.westroxbury.ma.boston.comcast.net names a town. Since you meant mtr on both sides, the point is moot. I'll drop it.
Throughput: 7.5 hours, not 29

2,000 traces in 7m 18s at -concurrency 50 is 4.57 traces/sec. For ~123k distinct on-premises addresses that is about 7.5 hours, not the 29 I projected. My estimate assumed 50 concurrent at mtr's nominal 5-cycle duration; in practice most traces finish far faster. Raising concurrency further is probably unnecessary — and before raising it, note that three defects mean much of this run was wasted work.
Defect 1: the "carrier node" is usually the landmark's own server

This is the one that breaks the method.

[1/2000]  34.174.18.13   -> last_hop=34.174.18.13(#6)   13.18.174.34.bc.googleusercontent.com
[7/2000]  162.241.224.125-> last_hop=162.241.224.125(#10) box5184.bluehost.com
[4/2000]  158.51.40.117  -> last_hop=158.51.40.117(#9)  158-51-40-117.brownrice.com

A landmark is a web server, and it answers ICMP. So the trace reaches it, the final responding hop is the destination, and classifyHops accepts it because a hostname like box5184.bluehost.com matches no exclusion and no customer marker. The recorded "last carrier node" is the landmark itself.

That is unusable for convergence. You cannot match a probe range's carrier node against a landmark's own web server. By eye this is somewhere between a third and a half of the 2,000 rows.

Range targets hid this, because a random address in a range almost never answers, so the trace dies short and the last responding hop really is a carrier router. The fix is the same for both sources and is correct in general: a hop whose address equals the address being traced is never a carrier node. When the destination answers, the carrier node is the hop before it, which is already in the trace — the data was collected, the wrong hop was chosen.

Visible proof the good data is there, from the same run:

[38/2000]  73.60.182.115 -> 162.151.191.122 po-1-rur202.westroxbury.ma.boston.comcast.net
[37/2000]  70.88.255.56  -> 68.86.90.61     be-1004-arsc1.woburn.ma.boston.comcast.net
[173/2000] 50.219.135.124-> 24.124.203.82   lg-2-soag01.lynn.ma.boston.comcast.net
[188/2000] 50.200.190.235-> 24.124.204.234  lg-2-soag09.maynard.ma.boston.comcast.net
[572/2000] 74.10.73.135  -> 96.110.118.34   be-2-1-ssag14.peabody.ma.boston.comcast.net

Westroxbury, Woburn, Lynn, Maynard, Peabody. Comcast encodes the town in the PTR. That is exactly the signal the method needs, and it is Massachusetts.
Defect 2: you are tracing addresses that rule 2 excludes

onpremises has never been applied — you have only run --dry-run — so the stored column still reflects the pre-provider state. The run is full of CDN and hosting addresses that rule 2 now makes false:

104.21.x, 172.67.x, 104.16.x, 104.26.x (Cloudflare), googleusercontent.com, secureserver.net, cloudfront.net, unifiedlayer.com, dreamhost.com, hostgator.com, weebly.com, vultrusercontent.com, linodeusercontent.com, inmotionhosting.com, contaboserver.net.

The Cloudflare ones all terminate at 152.193.179.74 customer.alter.net, one Verizon customer-edge router, which is why excluded-internal is so frequent. Your own dry run says 16,101 currently-true rows will flip, about 12% of the pass. Apply onpremises before the full run.
Defect 3: backbone cores accepted as carrier nodes

Many reached results land on transit cores: be2765.ccr41.ord03.atlas.cogentco.com, ae2.2.edge1.Chicago10.net.lumen.tech, ae12.er1.hoi1.us.zip.zayo.com, 100ge0-35.core11.fmt2.he.net, phx-b9-link.ip.twelve99.net. alter.net, level3.net, gtt.net, as6453.net and sprintlink.net are already excluded; Cogent, Lumen, Zayo, HE and Telia's twelve99.net are not.

The fan-out guard would reject these anyway, so they are not a correctness risk, but they waste traces. I am not adding them unilaterally, because Cogent is ambiguous in a way worth your ruling: ccr41/agr21/ccr91 are core and aggregation routers, but nr11.b023948-0.ind01 and nr61.b002250-1.bos01 carry a b###### building or customer identifier, so some Cogent hostnames are genuinely customer-edge. A blanket cogentco.com exclusion would discard those. Same shape for Zayo, where .IDIA-403920-ZYO.zip.zayo.com is a customer circuit ID while ae12.er1.hoi1.us is core.

My proposal, for review: exclude lumen.tech, he.net, twelve99.net, and for Cogent and Zayo exclude by router-role regex on the core forms rather than by domain. Say the word and I'll draft it.

cp geo/overture_fetch/ovt_resolve_hosts.py ~/geo/overture_fetch/

psql -d postgres -c "delete from ovt_places_usa_ip_trace where last_hop_ip = ip"
psql -d postgres -c "select count(distinct ip_address) as ma_landmarks from ovt_places_usa where onpremises and ip_address is not null and left(lpad(btrim(overture_zip::text),5,'0'),3) = '021'"

That count tells you the size of the Massachusetts pass before you start it. Then:

/var/trugeo/last_carrier_node/bin/last_carrier_node -source landmarks -zip-prefix 021 -n 5000 -concurrency 50 -ipv4-only -pause-file /var/log/trugeo/probe.paused
psql -d postgres -f geo/landmark_carrier_node.sql

Section 1b gives the waste figures and section 4 the fan-out histogram, which is the number that decides whether the method works. On the Foursquare/OSM/Wikidata expansion to ~44,000 inhabited ZIPs: at 4.57 traces/sec the tracing itself scales fine, so the constraint will be the fan-out distribution rather than throughput — if a Comcast rur node serves one ZIP you get ZIP precision, and if it serves eight you get a town. That is what section 4 on the Massachusetts data will tell us, on real carriers, before any of the new sources are ingested.

Est. Credits Used: 17.16

Elapsed Time: 7m 3s

Exclude the landmark's IP from the search for carrier node in the mtr output. Note that the landmark's IP (or the IP of any destination) sometimes responds to ICMP and other times does not. Identification of the last carrier node should work in both cases.

As we have discussed, business customers often have more than one CPE node in mtr output (I've seen two and there may be cases of three). The CPE node closest to the carrier interconnection, and possibly any farther nodes, usually have domain names in the customer's domain. Furthermore, the last carrier node sometimes doesn't have a domain name; we found cases in business private-Internet-access connections.

If the second node from Mint30 (Verizon FIOS) does not respond, retry up to 3 times. Provide the percentage of all mtr calls in which this happens, and the percentage where the second node does not respond all 3 times. We may need to increase the retry maximum. Eventually this entire system will be migrated to AWS where rate limits at the first carrier node will not occur.

The percentages: I can't give them to you yet

The instrumentation didn't exist, so the data isn't in the 301-row run. I've added it rather than estimate. After the next pass, section 1c reports both:

    share of individual mtr calls where hop 2 was silent
    share of addresses where it was silent on every attempt

The second is the one that tells you whether 3 is enough. If it's near the per-call rate cubed, the failures are independent and raising the limit helps. If it's much higher, the silence is persistent for those destinations and raising it won't.

The only adjacent figure computable from your log is 15 of 301 (5.0%) that ended unreachable with the nearest resolved hop at position 2 — but hop 2 did answer in those, so it's a different measurement.
What the run showed

The self-trace fix worked: zero self-traces in 301. But with the destination excluded, the hop chosen instead was the customer's own router, exactly as you described:

18.9.108.52    -> 18.0.193.110  oc11-755-rtr-1-backbone-rtr-1.mit.edu    SAME /8
140.247.105.21 -> 140.247.2.50  core-np-gw-vl412.fas.harvard.edu         SAME /16
130.64.212.93  -> 130.64.1.58   mky-n9k-01-x-mky-core-pri.net.tufts.edu  SAME /16
204.167.92.20  -> 204.167.92.26 gatehouse.cambridgema.gov                SAME /16

Eight of ten sampled. Now the destination's registered domain is taken from its own reverse DNS and any hop sharing it is skipped as CPE. On MIT the answer moves from MIT's backbone router to lmagw1-te-7-3-core.nox.org, Northern Crossroads, their actual upstream.

Unnamed carrier nodes are now accepted, labelled reached-unnamed so they stay separable. Finding that case required restructuring the selection: the old "nearest resolved hop is at position 2 or 3" rule fired first and returned unreachable even when hops further out had responded without resolving. Those are different conditions and conflating them hid exactly the case you asked for.
One limitation I can't close by name alone

An unnamed hop can't be tested for customer ownership by domain. If a business's own routers are unnamed, reached-unnamed may still be sitting on one. The test that settles it is whether the hop's BGP origin AS equals the destination's — MIT is AS3 holding 18.0.0.0/8, so 18.0.193.110 behind an 18.9.x destination is unambiguously inside the customer.

So I've started storing the full hop list as jsonb. Two passes have now been spent discovering the choice rule was wrong, each costing hours, while the hop list costs about a kilobyte per address. Section 1d runs the origin-AS check over it, and the node can be re-chosen by SQL instead of by re-probing. That's the lesson from this sequence: the trace is expensive and the classification is cheap, so the classification shouldn't be welded to the probe.

We cannot apply landmark ZIP codes to DHCP IPs in the same ZIP code because the dynamic and static IP ranges for the same geographic area will typically be separate, to permit automation to relocate the dynamic range elsewhere while the static range stays with the customer. Your reasoning seems to suggest we could match landmarks (static addresses) to dynamic addresses (biddable media-consuming households) by range (prefix). We cannot. Whether we can match by ASN is a very prescient question, the answer to which may become clear from the Massachusetts run. But carriers' ASNs immediately adjacent to CPE are, as far as I know, much wider geographically than one ZIP code or cluster of ZIP codes; if this is so, matching on ASN would break the ZIP-code-level targeting.

Merged as ed1254e. I've also recorded the sudo -v rule as a standing preference.
Hop 2: measured zero
	
mtr calls	312
hop 2 silent	0 (0.00%)
addresses silent on every attempt	0 (0.00%)
mean attempts	1.00

The retry never fired. No need to raise the maximum. The silence that does occur is at hop 1 and at hops 4–5, not at the Verizon node — one stored hop list shows hop 1 absent and hop 2 answering at 6.2ms.
The prefix is not a link, and you're right that I framed it loosely

The header now states it: static landmark ranges and dynamic household ranges are kept separate precisely so the dynamic range can be relocated, so a landmark's prefix says nothing about nearby households. The matching was always node-to-node, but ip_address_range and the section-8 merge made it look like prefix matching was on the table. Those are provenance columns, not join keys, and the file now says so.
Your ASN question: right for transit, still open for retail

Of 235 reached landmarks:
node operator	nodes	router IPs	share
transit / backbone	152	44	64.7%
retail access	38	35	16.2%
hosting / other	45	29	19.1%

Two Cogent routers carried 37% of the entire sample:

be3664.agr22.bos01  63 addresses spanning  7 ZIPs  02110-02215
be3255.ccr32.bos01  24 addresses spanning 11 ZIPs  02114-02215

Boston metro aggregation routers. So yes — for transit-reached landmarks the node is metro-wide.

But the decisive objection is different and doesn't depend on breadth at all. A transit circuit to a business carries no household traffic whatsoever. Those landmarks can't anchor a ZIP for any household however narrow their node turns out to be. Two thirds of the sample is disqualified on that ground alone, before granularity enters the argument.

The retail nodes are the opposite shape. Comcast names them by town: westroxbury, cambridge, framingham, norwood, peabody, plymouth, foxboro, exeter, derry, londonderry. A business on Comcast Business in Framingham is on the same access plant as Comcast residential in Framingham — the convergence the method actually needs. Their breadth is not measured, because this sample holds roughly one landmark per Comcast node, so there's nothing to spread.

That changes what the next run should be. Measuring retail-node breadth needs more landmarks per town, not more towns — which means a national pass is the wrong next step, and 021xx was arguably already too broad a slice to answer it.
Section 4 was measuring two things at once

My fault. It counted ZIPs among all places behind a node, but one address serves many places, so it reported lumen.tech at 1,108 ZIPs across four addresses. That measures the sharing, not the node. Section 4b now measures breadth only on addresses mapping to a single ZIP; 4c reports the shared ones as a candidate provider list and surfaced LinkNow Media, a website builder at 924 ZIPs across 9 addresses, missing from provider_names.
Unexplained, and I'm not going to guess

Section 1d reports the node inside the destination's own origin AS for 38.7% of reached and 58.3% of reached-unnamed, after the domain-based CPE fix. I haven't established why. A plausible cause is landmarks on carrier-owned address space, where sharing an AS with the node is normal rather than an error — but that's a hypothesis, not a finding. The query to list examples is in the file.
Two other figures

The full national pass is 2.2 hours, not 7.5: recomputing onpremises for real dropped the distinct on-premises addresses to 28,324 from the 123k I'd been assuming.

15,963 ZIPs currently have at least one on-premises landmark, against your target of ~44,000 inhabited. That's the coverage baseline before Foursquare and OSM.

No new trace needed — sections 4b, 4c and 4d re-read the 312 rows you already have, and carrier_node_class is seeded for your review. Read 4d first: it tells you how much of the pass survives the retail-only rule.

Then the question I'd put to you before any further tracing: should the next pass restrict to landmarks already known to sit behind a retail access network, so we get many landmarks per town and can finally measure whether a Comcast rur node is one ZIP or five? That is the number the whole method rests on, and nothing measured so far constrains it.

Elapsed Time: 5m 16s

CGNAT provides only DMA-level accuracy. We should treat transit providers like Cogent, Lumen, and Zayo similarly (although distinguishing them from mobile CGNAT for auditability). Use field ip2city_dbiplite_probe_tbl.likely_mobile_cgnat ; change its datatype to varchar2(1) and rename it to mobile_transit with values of 'm' for mobile, 't' for transit, or 'f' for fixed (coaxial, fiber, hybrid or DSL).

Business IPs do consume biddable media, whether at-work or in campus housing. We should not rule them out.

Section 4b reverses what I told you last turn

The corrected measurement, on landmark addresses that map to a single ZIP:

    node_domain    | router_ips | landmark_addresses | worst_zips | mean_zips | routers_serving_one_zip
-------------------+------------+--------------------+------------+-----------+------------------------
 cogentco.com      |         15 |                 89 |          6 |      1.53 |          13 of 15
 comcast.net       |         14 |                 16 |          3 |      1.14 |          13 of 14

Cogent's routers are nearly as ZIP-specific as Comcast's. My "7 and 11 Boston ZIPs on one Cogent router" was an artefact of shared addresses, not node breadth. 13 of 15 Cogent routers serve exactly one ZIP. One spans 6 — almost certainly the Cambridge university cluster.

So on the node-granularity question your suspicion and my confirmation of it were both wrong, and the measurement I built to test it says so. Transit nodes are narrow. The reason to treat them as DMA is the one you gave — a transit circuit carries no households — not breadth.
Rule 3a is admitting ISP web hosting at scale

Section 4c's registrants are the real find:
address	ZIPs	places	registrant
24.38.41.117	903	1065	Cablevision Lightpath
46.110.128.82	628	676	Metronet
64.135.100.26	520	585	BroadbandONE
207.120.44.73	512	598	Level 3 Parent
24.255.96.229	344	411	Cox Communications
107.0.132.30	139	160	Comcast Cable
216.21.239.197	173	180	Boost Mobile

All are in isp_names, so rule 3a made them onpremises = true unconditionally. These are ISP shared web hosting — one datacenter address serving hundreds of customer websites across the country. The Synergy Networks argument, at scale, through a hole I left open: rule 3a is a hard true that bypasses every ZIP test.

The detector gives a better rule than any name list: an address whose landmark places span more than N ZIPs is a shared host, whatever its registrant. Per-address, measurable, no research required. Twelve addresses in a 312-address sample carry over 200 ZIPs each. I'd suggest adding it as rule 2b, before 3a. Your call on N — the distribution is bimodal, so anything from 3 to 10 separates cleanly.
What I built

mobile_transit varchar(1) replacing likely_mobile_cgnat, on all four tables, with m/t/f/NULL. The substantive part is your framing: it's an accuracy tier, not an exclusion. Every filter that used the boolean to discard now either admits only f for ZIP assignment or counts the tier. NULL is kept distinct from f because the unnamed-node case genuinely cannot be classified.

Transit comes from a new transit_domain rule type in traceroute_hostname_rules, so the Go tool and the SQL backfill read one list. Nineteen domains. Cogent and Zayo are included by domain with the cost written down: their b-number and IDIA- hostnames are customer edge and will be mislabelled t. Given 4b, that mislabelling now matters more than I thought — those are narrow routers being demoted to DMA. att.net is left out entirely for the same reason.

This had to be atomic: three deployed binaries write the column, and a rename leaves a window where a running one references a column that no longer exists.

Not built: the ip-api accuracy comparison

I prioritised the schema change because it couldn't be split across three binaries, and I'd rather tell you that than ship a half-tested network tool beside it.

The design, for your approval or redirection: a small tool reading on-premises landmark addresses with -zip-prefix, calling ip-api at the existing 45/min, writing to ovt_places_usa_ip_api, then a comparison grouped by isp against overture_zip as ground truth — exact ZIP, adjacent ZIP, same zip3, same state, wrong state. 312 Massachusetts addresses is about seven minutes. It's a genuinely clean validation because the landmark ZIP is known, which is unusual.

One caveat worth raising before it runs: section 4c means a good share of those 312 addresses are ISP hosting in a datacenter, so ip-api will be "wrong" about them for a reason that has nothing to do with its accuracy on real subscriber addresses. The comparison should exclude the shared addresses first, or report them separately. Otherwise it will understate ip-api and we'll draw the wrong conclusion about RCN versus FIOS.

If a transit node is narrow, and maps to one ZIP or a cluster of adjacent ZIPs, make it available for ZIP-level targeting. It may carry traffic from institutional housing or at-work media use.

Check each last carrier node for fanout and report cases of fanout beyond one ZIP or a cluster of adjacent ZIPs. For example, Comcast serves West Roxbury through a Brockton node, an hour away and with dramatically different demographics. Likewise, it serves Lynn through a Woburn node, a milder version of the same targeting-defeating transit across huge gaps in demography. Treat your assertion that Comcast is nearly ZIP-specific with extreme caution; I wish it was correct, but the evidence just listed suggests we test.

"Rule 3a is admitting ISP web hosting at scale": You got there before me, but I think deeming "an address whose landmark places span more than N ZIPs [as] a shared host, whatever its registrant" may be too crude. I propose that an IP address that serves multiple (more than one) ZIP clusters that do not border each other be deemed "hosting", and that we use this definition rather than hardcoding registrant names in the providers table. Three failures of mine in that run

The transit classification silently did nothing. CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS skipped the existing table, so the UNIQUE (rule_type, pattern) never reached it, both ON CONFLICT inserts aborted, and zero transit_domain rules loaded. That is why you saw UPDATE 0 / UPDATE 0 and f | 312 | 100.0. psql reports the error and carries on, so it looked like a clean run. I had anticipated exactly this hazard for the CHECK constraint and wrote an explicit ALTER for it, then failed to do the same for the UNIQUE.

ip2city_dbiplite_traceroute_backup_tbl was missing from my table list. It still had the old boolean.

I did a rename when you asked for an end result. You were right and the cost is concrete, not stylistic: with the old column renamed away, a row-by-row verification of the mapping on those four tables is no longer possible. The counts are consistent (2,082,217 f, 15,653 m) but that is not the check you asked for, and it cannot be recovered. Section 6 does the backup table the right way — add, populate, verify, drop — with the DROP left commented, and records the pattern for future column changes.
My Comcast claim is withdrawn, and you were right to distrust it

Section 4b reported comcast.net at 14 router IPs with 16 landmark addresses. That is 1.14 landmarks per router. A node with one landmark behind it cannot show more than one ZIP whatever its real breadth, so "13 of 14 serving one ZIP" was an arithmetic consequence of sample size, not a measurement. Cogent at 5.9 landmarks per router was only marginally better, and its addresses are dominated by a few universities each sitting in one ZIP.

Nothing in that data constrains node breadth for either operator. I should have read the two columns together before asserting anything.

And a related error you've exposed. I treated the town in po-1-rur201.westroxbury.ma.boston.comcast.net as geographic signal. It records where the router is. West Roxbury served through Brockton refutes that directly. The hostname is an identity for matching and nothing else — which is how the assignment code actually works, so the design was fine and my commentary was wrong.
What I built

Fan-out measured in disjoint ZIP clusters via connected components over zip_adjacency, not raw ZIP counts. One cluster is one contiguous area however many ZIPs; two or more are separate places. Your two cases both reject correctly in test: West Roxbury + Brockton → 2 clusters, Lynn + Woburn → 2 clusters. A multi-site clinic across adjacent ZIPs is spared. Plus a distance screen flagging any node spanning over 15 miles, using db-ip centroids.

Every query prints landmarks_at_node beside the fan-out, and under three landmarks is labelled unmeasured rather than clean.

Narrow transit nodes are now ZIP-eligible. Width is the test, not operator identity — a Cogent node with three contiguous ZIPs passes as zip-level in the test suite.

Your cluster definition for hosting is better than my N-ZIPs rule and it's implemented. One limit worth knowing before retiring provider_names: it needs two or more landmarks at an address to see any spread, so a CDN address carrying exactly one landmark passes as on-premises. On the 312-address sample most provider addresses carried many places, but that's a property of that sample. The name list still covers the single-landmark case.
Critique of your plan

ip-api for Massachusetts: agree, with one sequencing caveat. Section 5 shows a large share of those 312 addresses are ISP web hosting in a datacenter. ip-api will be "wrong" about them for reasons unrelated to its accuracy on subscriber addresses. Run the hosting classification first and exclude or separate them, or the RCN-versus-FIOS comparison will be contaminated.

Upper Peninsula: right instinct, wrong instrument. The UP is the correct kind of second site — nodes genuinely sit in adjacent ZIPs there. But it has roughly 300,000 people across 42,000 km², so landmark density is very low, which means few landmarks per node: precisely the underpowering that just invalidated my Comcast claim. It would test adjacency tolerance and tell you nothing about fan-out. It also has almost no Comcast — mostly Charter, Frontier and small independents — so it cannot test the operator you're actually worried about.

The deeper point: site selection is no longer the right lever. It was, when I thought the full pass was 29 hours. It isn't: onpremises recomputed to 28,324 distinct addresses, which at the measured 3.5 traces/sec is 2.2 hours for the entire country. Trace everything, then slice analytically. That maximises landmarks-per-node everywhere at once, removes the site-selection judgement entirely, and lets the data tell you which rural areas have the adjacency problem rather than you nominating the UP in advance.

I'd put the ip-api comparison after the national pass for the same reason — ground truth is better once hosting addresses are identified from full-density cluster data.

What I found researching the sources

Row count is the wrong measure. The chain resolves a website to an IP and decides onpremises from that IP's registrant, so N places sharing one domain yield one landmark address. Measured on live loads: IPEDS 6,075 rows → 5,411 hosts (89.1% unique), 4,241 ZIPs; OSM Rhode Island 1,958 rows → 1,908 hosts (97.4%). Massachusetts has 15,132 OSM features with both tags against your 312 Overture on-premises addresses.

Three rejections, each checked rather than guessed:

    IMLS has no URL at all. The outlet file has ZIP and no web column; the administrative-entity file's only web-ish field among 192 columns is WEBVISIT, a count of visits.
    NPS is not worth the API key. Every park is an nps.gov URL, so ~470 parks collapse to one host — which your own cluster rule would then flag as hosting. Implemented anyway, documented as not worth running.
    Wikidata P281 looks like the right property and isn't: on US items it returns city-level ranges like 10000–10499. I used P6375 street address instead, where the ZIP sits in the text in exactly the freeform shape your ZIP step already parses.

Two defects my own testing caught: IPEDS ships a UTF-8 BOM, which made DictReader["UNITID"] return None and silently collapsed the load to 1 row of 6,075. Fixed, and load_rows now refuses outright when more than half the ids are blank — that guard is the durable part. Wikidata's query service was rate-limiting to 1 req/min during an active outage, so the backoff honours Retry-After and waits 65s on a bare 429.

One thing to expect in the crosswalk: for-profit college chains and retail chains share one domain across many ZIPs (paulmitchell.edu 96 ZIPs, locations.dunkindonuts.com 40). I deliberately did not filter those at load time — they're what the disjoint-cluster rule exists to catch, and filtering them here would create a second, different definition of hosting.

The token: what I got wrong

I conflated two different things — a name you invent and type, and a value Hugging Face generates and you copy. Answering your three questions directly:

    "Where is the hf_ value?" It does not exist yet. Hugging Face creates it after you submit the form. It appears on screen once, with a copy button.
    "Where in the dialogue is it pasted or copied from?" Nothing is pasted into the dialogue. You copy from the screen that appears after you press the create button.
    "What is the name of the new token?" A label you make up. It has no technical function — it only lets you identify and revoke that token later. Type trugeo.

Step by step

1. Go to https://huggingface.co/join. Enter email, password, username. Confirm the verification email.

2. Signed in, go to https://huggingface.co/datasets/foursquare/fsq-os-places. A grey box says you must agree to share your contact information. Tick the checkbox, press the Agree and access repository button. Access is immediate.

3. Go to https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens and press Create new token (older UI: New token).

4. The form has exactly two things you fill in:
field	what to do
Token type / role	Choose Read. Not Fine-grained, not Write.
Token name	Type trugeo

5. Press Create token.

6. Now the hf_ value appears — a single long string beginning hf_, shown in a box with a copy icon beside it and a warning that it won't be shown again. Press the copy icon. That is the only place it ever appears. If you navigate away without copying it, delete the token and repeat from step 3.

7. In your terminal, run this and paste the token at the prompt. It won't echo, and it stays out of your shell history:

read -rsp 'Paste HF token then press Enter: ' HF_TOKEN && export HF_TOKEN && echo
printf 'export HF_TOKEN=%s
' "$HF_TOKEN" >> ~/.hf_token && chmod 600 ~/.hf_token

8. Check it before starting a 10 GB download. This requests one kilobyte:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}
' -r 0-1023 -L -H "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN" 'https://huggingface.co/datasets/foursquare/fsq-os-places/resolve/main/release/dt=2026-10-15/places/parquet/places_000000.parquet'

206 means it works. 401 means the token didn't reach the server — redo step 7. 403 means step 2 wasn't completed. 404 means that release has rotated; run python3 fsq_fetch.py releases.

In any new shell afterwards: source ~/.hf_token

The fan-out run: your hypothesis is confirmed

Your numbers reconcile exactly to the known corpus — 28,324 addresses and 120,154 places — so the run is internally consistent.

Comcast is definitively not ZIP-specific. Of 174 measurable Comcast nodes, 18 are ZIP-level and 156 reject (89.7%). At 4.64 landmarks per node this is above the power threshold, so it is a real measurement, averaging 3.31 disjoint clusters per node. West Roxbury-via-Brockton and Lynn-via-Woburn were not anomalies; they are the national pattern. My withdrawn claim is now affirmatively dead, not merely unsupported.

But first, the honest caveat. Mean landmarks per node is 2.66 with a median of 1 — below the threshold of 3 I set in advance. Only 21% of nodes are measurable. What rescues the analysis is that those 1,297 nodes hold 64.3% of all landmarks (10,554 of 16,425), so the conclusions cover most of the landmark mass even though they cover few nodes.

The operational headline is poor. Of measured landmarks, only 17.8% (1,883 of 10,554) sit behind a node narrow enough for ZIP targeting.

The genuinely narrow operators are research and education networks, which I had not predicted:
operator	nodes	mean landmarks	mean clusters	zip-level	rejected
oar.net (Ohio academic)	13	7.46	1.31	10	3
cenic.net (California R&E)	20	6.25	1.75	13	7
comcast.net	173	4.64	3.31	17	156
cogentco.com	201	10.75	5.35	20	181
charter.com	132	5.39	3.89	12	120

R&E nodes serve one campus each, so they are ZIP-narrow for a structural reason. That makes university landmarks the most ZIP-targetable population you have, which supports the earlier decision to keep universities as landmarks.

Rule 3a is worse than expected, and now measured. 4,605 addresses are hosting by the cluster rule, holding 61,653 places. Of those, 4,427 addresses / 60,903 places are admitted solely because the registrant is in isp_names — that is 50.7% of the entire 120,154-place corpus. The density signature confirms it: hosting addresses carry 13.4 places each against 2.5 for genuine on-premises. And 181 "too wide to cluster" addresses alone hold 32,349 places, 27% of everything.

Two further defects in the data, which I am flagging rather than acting on:

    sdnet.net is tier f (fixed) while showing 34 ZIPs across 33 clusters. South Dakota Network is an aggregator; the 19-domain transit_domain list misses it. The list is hand-curated, and this run suggests replacing it with a measured rule — high cluster count across many landmarks is transit behaviour — rather than extending the list by hand. That is a design change I would want your view on.
    Videotron Ltée, a Quebec ISP, holds 45 addresses / 2,855 places in US landmark data. That points to a country-filtering gap upstream, not a classification error.

The decision I need from you

You proposed the cluster definition precisely to replace hardcoded registrant names. The evidence now supports it, but the cost is large enough that I won't apply it unilaterally: setting onpremises = false wherever address_hosting_tbl.verdict is hosting would remove 50.7% of places while removing only 16.3% of addresses.

I think that is correct — the removed addresses average 13.4 places each, which is not what a single building looks like. But it halves the corpus, so confirm before I implement it.

Merged (d2055f6).
The 502s are not mtr

They came from the Overpass API inside lm_fetch.py osm-overpass. mtr isn't involved in that tool at all — it only appears in last_carrier_node. Overpass 502s are transient server load, and my retry recovered them: 15,238 rows loaded on the third attempt.

But there is a real defect, and it's mine. Wikidata answered a 429 with Retry-After: 1000, and I honoured it literally — which parks the run for 17 minutes with no output, indistinguishable from a hang. Sleeps are now capped at 120s; beyond that it reports the service is rate-limiting and to re-run later. Press Ctrl-C on the current one if it's still sitting there; nothing else is affected, and your IPEDS and OSM loads already committed.
HF_TOKEN in .bashrc

Run once. The guard makes it safe to run repeatedly:

grep -q hf_token ~/.bashrc || printf '
[ -r ~/.hf_token ] && . ~/.hf_token
' >> ~/.bashrc

The token stays in ~/.hf_token at mode 600 and .bashrc only sources it, so .bashrc remains safe to show or copy.
The hosting rule, per address

Southwest Cyberport and Synergy Networks are why this had to be per-address rather than per-registrant. Excluding either by name discards its genuine on-premises places; admitting either by name lets its hosting farm in. That is precisely why both have sat in neither isp_names nor provider_names.

Each address is judged on its own ZIP-cluster fan-out. Disjoint clusters means a hosting farm whoever owns it; one contiguous area means a premises whoever owns it. A registrant doing both gets each address judged separately.

Section 2 of the rule finds these companies from the data rather than from a list — on fixtures it returns exactly your two. Section 4c proves each keeps its premises while losing its hosting:

     registrant      | still_onpremises | excluded_as_hosting | zips_still_served
 Southwest Cyberport |                1 |                   2 |                 1
 Synergy Networks    |                1 |                   2 |                 1

A new onpremises_reason column records which rule decided, because a hosting-rule false and a registrant-rule false are not the same claim.
One table

landmarks_usa, keyed on (source, source_id), with a common core plus source_attrs jsonb so nothing any source carries is lost. The three import tables stay untouched as raw imports — the migration only reads them. Loaders still differ, as you said; only the destination is shared.

Two decisions worth flagging:

    Only rows with a website migrate. A place with no website can never be a landmark, so ~11M permanently ineligible Overture rows stay in ovt_places_usa rather than costing scan time forever. The migration prints eligible_in_source beside migrated so you can verify nothing eligible was dropped.
    Completed RDAP is carried over, not recomputed — your 543,336 IPs and ~20 hours of lookups come across, so the chain resumes.

psql -d postgres -f onpremises_hosting_rule.sql

One caveat before you apply the rule

address_hosting_tbl was built by node_fanout.sql from ovt_places_usa only. Applied now, the rule covers Overture addresses correctly but will not yet judge the 275,517 Foursquare or 21,313 OSM/IPEDS places, because those have no RDAP or cluster verdict yet. The sensible order is: run the chain on landmarks_usa, rebuild address_hosting_tbl from it, then apply the rule. Rerunning the rule is idempotent, so applying it now and again later is safe — it just won't be complete on the first pass.

Also still open: the Videotron rows (2,855 places from a Quebec ISP) point to a country-filtering gap upstream, and sdnet.net is tier f while showing 33 disjoint clusters. The second suggests replacing the hand-curated 19-domain transit list with a measured rule, since high cluster count across many landmarks is transit behaviour. I'd want your view before changing that.
Steering
Used your naming of Southwest Cyberport and Synergy Networks directly rather than guessing — I had deliberately not named them. They became the test fixtures for the per-address rule, which reproduces both as one hosting address plus one on-premises address each, and section 2b of `onpremises_hosting_rule.sql` reports both by name. Section 2 also finds this class of registrant from the data generally, so the rule doesn't depend on the two names being known.

Merged (a15cdcb).
On the 120s cap — you were right to push

I did not know 120s was any service's interval. It was a round number I picked, which is exactly the kind of invented threshold that shouldn't be in the code.

The only rate-limit interval any of these services has actually stated is WDQS's "1 req / min", in its own 429 body. So 60s is the shortest cap that still lets every rate limit I've observed recover on the next attempt. The Overpass 502s carried no Retry-After at all and recovered at 15s and 30s, well inside it. Nothing observed demands between 60 and 120, so the extra 60 bought nothing. Reduced to 60s, and now settable with --max-backoff.

Then range-to-ZIP

cd /home/boris/geo/src/claude/geo/landmarks
psql -d postgres -f range2zip.sql

This is the piece you asked for. It matches the landmark side and the range side at the node, and writes range2zip_tbl keyed (network, zip) — so a single range serving several ZIPs produces several rows, with zips_at_range on each. Fixture result:

     network      |  zip  | match_method  | landmark_sources | zips | clusters | verdict
 203.0.113.0/25   | 02116 | node_ip       | overture         |    3 |        1 | zip: one contiguous area of 3
 203.0.113.0/25   | 02119 | node_ip       | foursquare       |    3 |        1 | zip: one contiguous area of 3
 203.0.113.128/25 | 02116 | node_hostname | overture         |    3 |        1 | zip: one contiguous area of 3
 198.51.100.0/24  | 01901 | node_ip       | osm              |    2 |        2 | disjoint: 2 areas

Two design points worth your attention. Node IP is the strong match; hostname equality is a fallback, because two traces often end on different interfaces of the same router — that's the 203.0.113.128/25 row. And disjoint matches are written and tagged, not dropped: a range behind a node spanning unconnected areas isn't located by that match, so range2zip_usable_v filters them out while the table keeps them for audit.

One ordering caveat: run range2zip.sql only after the chain has set onpremises on landmarks_usa, since it reads onpremises IS TRUE. Run now against the empty table it will produce zero rows, the same way the hosting rule just did.

I'd already finished testing `range2zip.sql`, so I pushed it in the same PR rather than splitting, and sequenced it after the migration and chain since it depends on `onpremises` being set — which is also why your `onpremises_hosting_rule.sql` run returned zero rows.

3 tools

Both questions found real defects. Merged as 1481fc3.
The limit

You're right — we want everything, and --limit 50000 was a number I picked without knowing the total. I've now measured it: 29,858 US Wikidata items carry both a street address (P6375) and a website (P856), of which 26,088 have a 5-digit ZIP. So the default happened not to truncate anything, but that was luck, not design. Default is now 0, meaning all.

It was also worse than arbitrary: --limit meant an absolute offset ceiling, so combined with --resume it did nothing at all. Resuming at offset 961 with --limit 500 saw 961 already past 500 and exited having merged zero — indistinguishable from a failure. That's what the "FAIL" in my own test turned out to be. It now counts rows fetched by that run.
The abort mechanism

There was one, but it was weak. There are now three, and none of them lose work:
mechanism	effect
--deadline-minutes N	stops the whole pull after N minutes, keeping every page merged
--max-backoff N	refuses a Retry-After longer than N seconds instead of sleeping
page failure	stops, keeps what's merged, names the other endpoint to try
But the serious bug was neither of those

Checking resumability found that a partial re-run went backwards. load_rows defaulted to replace=True: delete every row for the source, then COPY. A first run fetching 30,000 rows followed by a second managing only 20,000 before the service failed left you with 20,000 — losing 10,000. Under a rate limit that's the normal case, not an edge case. And because pagination always restarted at offset 0, repeated partial runs could never accumulate past wherever the service happened to cut out.

Batches now stage in a temp table and merge with ON CONFLICT, updating only the 15 load columns so enrichment the chain has already written survives.
And I've switched endpoints

WDQS is still rate-limiting to 1 request/minute and now 504s on even a COUNT. QLever (qlever.dev) is an independent index of the same Wikidata dump and answered that same COUNT in under a second. It's now the default; --endpoint wdqs remains for cross-checking.

I also added ORDER BY ?item, which isn't cosmetic — without it SPARQL OFFSET has no defined order, so pages can overlap or skip and resuming would be approximate rather than correct.

Live-verified end to end:

run 1 (--limit 1000)                    ->    961 rows
run 2 (--resume --limit 1000)           ->  1,839 rows   grew correctly
run 3 (unbounded, --deadline-minutes 1) -> 22,741 rows   21,692 merged, stopped cleanly
re-run of overlapping offsets           ->    961 -> 961  idempotent

The full 26,088 takes about two minutes.

One more bug surfaced only by running it: a Wikidata street address contains a literal newline, and inline COPY ... FROM STDIN is read line-by-line while psql hunts for the \. terminator — so correct CSV quoting still failed with unquoted newline found in data. Batches now go through a temp file read by client-side \copy.
So the command is simply

cd /home/boris/geo/src/claude && git pull origin main
cd geo/landmark_sources
python3 lm_fetch.py wikidata

If it stops for any reason, python3 lm_fetch.py wikidata --resume.

Worth noting QLever returned a transient 500 during one of my tests, so neither endpoint is perfectly reliable — which is exactly why resume and per-page merging now matter more than the limit ever did.

ip-api — it's far cheaper than I expected

The free /batch endpoint takes 100 addresses per request at 15 requests/minute, so 1,500/min against 45 for single calls. Your ~28,000 on-premises addresses take about 20 minutes, not 10 hours.

More importantly, /batch and /json have separate budgets — I measured X-Rl 12 and X-Rl 44 seconds apart. That removes the window problem ipapi_rate_test documents, where probe_batch already occupies ~53 minutes of every hour of the single-endpoint budget. Verify before committing:

cd /home/boris/geo/src/claude/geo/landmarks

If check-budget shows the two X-Rl values far apart and the dry-run time looks acceptable:

python3 landmarks_ip_api.py probe
python3 landmarks_ip_api.py compare

Two deliberate choices. It probes distinct addresses, not places — 122,110 places sit on far fewer addresses. And it excludes hosting addresses by default, because ip-api reports the host's location while our ZIP reports the tenant's; counting that as disagreement would blame the pipeline for a mismatch that is correct on both sides and would swamp the real signal.

Also note check_geo_ip-api's header comment saying batch is paid-only is out of date — it answered HTTP 200 unauthenticated.
Then range-to-ZIP

range2zip.sql is already built and tested. Before running it, check section 7 of the gap report: it counts how many on-premises addresses have actually been traced to a carrier node. The matching can only use traced landmarks, and your node_fanout_tbl had 16,425 landmarks across 6,169 nodes — so if that is well short of the ~28,000 on-premises addresses, the landmark side needs another last_carrier_node -source landmarks pass first to raise the match rate.

psql -d postgres -f geo/landmarks/range2zip.sql

It writes range2zip_tbl keyed (network, zip), so a range serving several ZIPs produces several rows with zips_at_range on each, and range2zip_usable_v filters out nodes whose ZIPs form disjoint clusters.

Before more sources: a finding that reframes the problem

Your 296,830 new rows moved onpremises = true from 120,154 to 122,110. +1,956. A 0.66% yield.

The chain is correct. onpremises needs the registrant ZIP at or next to the landmark's ZIP, and a business in a POI feed is usually on Squarespace, Wix or GoDaddy — so the registrant ZIP is the host's, not the premises'. It correctly rejects them.

So the question isn't which source has the most places. It's which source lists organisations that run their own web server at their own address. Business POI feeds are structurally poor landmark sources, and more of them won't help.
What I found for schools, libraries and local government

Local government: CISA's .gov registry is the best new candidate, and it's aimed precisely at sparse ZIPs. Open, no key, verified: 16,980 domains, of which 14,140 are local government — 9,256 City, 2,724 County, 1,125 Special district, 289 Tribal. It's a registry of municipalities, and small towns are municipalities. All 54 states/territories, 9,170 distinct city/state pairs:

VT:  94 domains / 87 towns   (of roughly 250 municipalities)
ME: 134 / 107     MT: 114 / 80     SD: 60 / 50     WY: 63 / 38

It has City and State but no ZIP — survivable, because your overture-zip locality fallback already assigns the unambiguous ZIP per locality and labels the provenance locality rather than postcode, so the weaker evidence stays visible. It should also do well on onpremises, since a town government's RDAP registrant is usually the town itself.

Schools and libraries: there is no national registry of their websites. Checked rather than assumed — NCES CCD for K-12 has zip_location and, across 52 fields, zero web/url/site fields. IMLS libraries have ZIP and, across 192 fields, only WEBVISIT, which is a count of visits. E-Rate carries neither. Both are authoritative address lists with no URL.

The practical route to schools and libraries is therefore OpenStreetMap, which has them with real ZIPs — and the national OSM pass is already built (osm-pbf) and has never been run. Massachusetts alone gave 15,238; Texas 52,269.
The probe service — RIPE Atlas

That's the one. I can't find where I raised it earlier, so I'm naming it as the likely match rather than claiming credit.

It will not fix landmark density, and I'd rather say so than sell it. 2,376 connected US probes against ~44,000 inhabited ZIPs, and heavily metro-clustered: 500 sampled probes fell into only 149 one-degree cells, led by SF Bay (45), DC (32), Seattle (25), LA (24). People who volunteer to host network probes live in cities — close to the opposite of what you need.

What it is genuinely worth is validating the core inference. You trace toward a landmark and treat the last carrier node as a proxy for the equipment a subscriber sits behind. An Atlas probe is a subscriber connection at a known location, so a traceroute from it reports that subscriber's real carrier node directly — independent of ip-api and of RDAP. 444 of 500 sampled probes expose a public IPv4, all carry coordinates, and the measurement API works with a free key.

Too few to be a corpus; more than enough to test a method. And it would catch West Roxbury-via-Brockton cases with a known subscriber location rather than an inferred one.

Full writeup in geo/landmark_sources/sparse_zip_sources.md.

Thought (7)

Confirmed, and this is the real answer. Let me summarise what I measured.
No — and 16 cores is the wrong lever

CPU is not the bottleneck. Five lookups consumed 0.247s of user CPU in total, about 3ms per jq spawn across 15 spawns each. Your 16 cores are sitting idle; this is network-bound work.

ARIN scales badly with concurrency. I measured it directly:
threads	calls/sec	gain over 4
4	6.31	—
8	7.09	+12%
16	8.83	+40%
32	10.73	+70%

8× the threads buys 1.7× the throughput. That curve is server-side shaping, not client capacity.

And you are probably already shaped. Sequentially, single-threaded from here, rdap-lookup.sh averages 0.21s per call = 4.7 calls/sec. Your pipeline at 4 threads managed 4.25 calls/sec. Your four threads are delivering roughly my one.

Your previous run's failures support that. 5,502 of 53,235 failed (10.3%), and they came in bursts that failed fast — at the 16.2k mark, 800 attempts produced 16 successes in 16 seconds. Fast rejection, not timeouts. The bursts appeared at ~16k, ~32k and ~45k, which looks like a sustained-volume limit rather than a per-second one.

So raising threads risks converting slow successes into fast failures, and each failure costs a retry pass later.
Check this before deciding, because it's your evidence not mine

My sandbox is a different source IP from your server, so I cannot see what ARIN is doing to you. Your error log can:

cd /home/boris/geo/src/claude/geo
head -1 landmarks_usa_rdap_errors.csv
cut -d, -f3- landmarks_usa_rdap_errors.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -15

If that shows HTTP 429 or connection resets, you are rate-limited and more threads will make it worse. If it shows timeouts or DNS errors, there is headroom and 8–12 threads is reasonable.
What I would actually do

Don't kill the running job. It's resumable, but five hours of completed lookups are worth more than a 12% speedup on the remainder.

If the error log shows no 429s, 8 threads is a safe bump for the next run — but expect ~12%, not 4×:

python3 overture_fetch/ovt_resolve_hosts.py rdap --table landmarks_usa --rdap-threads 8

The lever that is actually large

ARIN's reply names the whole network, not just the IP:

handle      : NET-8-8-8-0-2
startAddress: 8.8.8.0
endAddress  : 8.8.8.255
cidr0_cidrs : [{'v4prefix': '8.8.8.0', 'length': 24}]

So once one IP in a network is looked up, every other IP in that same network needs no call at all — the registrant is identical by construction. On a 40-IP sample I got 28 distinct networks, 30% avoidable, and some ranges are enormous:

13.64.0.0  - 13.107.255.255   Microsoft
104.16.0.0 - 104.31.255.255   Cloudflare
23.192.0.0 - 23.223.255.255   Akamai

On landmark data this should save far more than 30%, because landmark IPs concentrate on exactly those shared hosts — which is the same clustering that produced your 0.66% onpremises yield. The current step caches per IP and therefore pays repeatedly for one answer.

That is a change to the rdap step: store the returned network range, and skip any IP already covered by a known range. It would cut the next full run substantially rather than this one. Say the word and I'll build it — it needs a rdap_networks cache table and a containment check before each call.

Two smaller notes while you wait: the heartbeat fix is merged, so pull before the next long run and you'll get still running, Ns elapsed lines during silent statements. And 871,668 of your rows are outside ARIN, which no amount of ARIN threading will resolve — those need the other RIRs, which the current script deliberately doesn't query.

Thought (1) + Tools (1)

My earlier command was wrong

I used -f3- but the file has exactly two columns, ip,error — so it printed 7,633 empty lines. That number is still useful: 7,633 error rows accumulated (the log is appended across runs, so it spans the previous run's 5,502 plus this one so far).

Run this instead. It extracts the HTTP status code, which is the thing that actually answers your question:

cd /home/boris/geo/src/claude/geo
cat > /tmp/diag.py <<'PY'
import csv, re, collections, sys, os
PATH = "landmarks_usa_rdap_errors.csv"
if not os.path.exists(PATH):
    sys.exit("not found: " + PATH)
http = collections.Counter()
kinds = collections.Counter()
total = 0
for row in csv.reader(open(PATH, newline="", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")):
    if len(row) < 2 or row[0] == "ip":
        continue
    total = total + 1
    e = row[1]
    m = re.search("HTTP ([0-9][0-9][0-9])", e)
    code = m.group(1) if m else None
    if code:
        http[code] = http[code] + 1
    k = re.sub("[0-9]+[.][0-9]+[.][0-9]+[.][0-9]+", "IP", e)
    k = re.sub("[0-9]+", "N", k)
    if code:
        k = k.replace("HTTP N", "HTTP " + code)
    kinds[k[:95]] = kinds[k[:95]] + 1
print("total error rows: " + format(total, ","))
print("")
print("HTTP status codes returned by ARIN:")
for c, n in http.most_common():
    print("    HTTP " + c + ": " + format(n, ","))
if not http:
    print("    none - no HTTP status in any error, so these are not ARIN rejections")
print("")
print("grouped failure kinds:")
for t, n in kinds.most_common(15):
    print("    " + format(n, ">8,") + "  " + t)
PY
python3 /tmp/diag.py

How to read the result

The script emits Error: ARIN RDAP returned HTTP <code> for <ip> on any non-200, so the status codes are recoverable from the log.

    Lots of HTTP 429 → you are rate-limited. Do not raise threads; consider lowering them.
    Lots of HTTP 503 → ARIN is shedding load. Same conclusion.
    Mostly HTTP 404 → those are registrant not found, not throttling, and they are not retryable usefully.
    Mostly curl: (28) Operation timed out → the script's own --max-time 15. Ambiguous: could be slow ARIN responses or throttling by stalling, which is how ip-api behaves. If this dominates, raising --rdap-timeout is more likely to help than raising threads.
    No HTTP codes at all → the failures are local, and threads are not the issue.

Unchanged recommendation until that output exists

Your 4 threads deliver 4.25 calls/sec; my single thread here does 4.7. You are getting one thread's worth of throughput from four, and my concurrency test showed 8× threads buys only 1.7× rate. So the ceiling is ARIN's, not your 16 cores — CPU use is about 50ms per lookup.

Don't kill the running job. Five hours of completed lookups is worth more than a 12% speedup on what remains.

One incidental check that came out clean: rdap-lookup.sh removes its /tmp/arin_payload.$$.json on both the success and curl-failure paths, so 76k calls won't litter /tmp.

Ran command

Merged (e23934e).
Why 122,953

The step selects lookup_status IS NULL OR lookup_status = 'lookup error'. lookup error was 317 before this run, so ~122,636 are brand-new distinct IPs — every new website host from the national OSM pass plus dotgov that resolved to an address. One call each. Nothing is being redone.
Yes, and threads were never the lever

The bottleneck is the TLS handshake. Each lookup spawns a fresh curl, so every call opens a new connection:

20 separate curl processes          3.833s = 0.192s per call
1 curl process reusing the socket   0.121s = 0.006s per call   -> 32x

One call breaks down as:

dns          0.001s
tcp connect  0.061s
tls          0.066s
-----------------------
setup        0.127s = 68% of the 0.188s total
query itself ~0.060s

68% of every call is setup, paid again on every IP. That also explains the earlier puzzle: 8× the threads returned only 1.7× the throughput, because each thread spent most of its time shaking hands rather than waiting on ARIN. Your 1.02s per call is dominated by this.

RDAP now runs in-process on one HTTPS connection per worker thread, kept alive. Verified 15/15 byte-identical to the script, and end-to-end through the rdap step 0 rows differed in url_location or lookup_status. Single-thread rate went 4.92 → 14.36 IPs/sec.
I'm retracting the optimisation I proposed earlier

I suggested caching ARIN network ranges so one lookup could cover every IP in the range. That is unsafe. ARIN nests allocations:

8.8.2.1 -> NET-8-0-0-0-1  8.0.0.0-8.8.3.255  Level 3 Parent, LLC
8.8.4.1 -> NET-8-8-4-0-2  8.8.4.0-8.8.4.255  Google LLC

Both share parent NET-8-0-0-0-0. Caching the provider's wide range and skipping IPs inside it would return the provider instead of the customer — exactly the distinction onpremises depends on. It would have degraded landmark detection while appearing to work. Don't build it.
What to do with the running job

It's resumable: completed IPs have lookup_status set, so a restart skips them and loses nothing but the in-flight batch.

cd /home/boris/geo/src/claude && git pull origin main

Then stop the current rdap step with Ctrl-C and restart it:

cd /home/boris/geo/src/claude/geo
python3 overture_fetch/ovt_resolve_hosts.py rdap --table landmarks_usa

Native is the default now. Keep --rdap-threads at 4 — the handshake was the constraint, and with it gone the remaining per-call cost is ARIN's actual response time, where my concurrency measurements showed the server shaping anyway.

If you want to confirm the gain before committing, the first progress line will tell you: you were at 3.94 IPs/sec, and anything materially above that is the reuse working.

Then continue with steps 4 through 7 as issued. One flag worth remembering: if any registrant text ever looks wrong after this, --rdap-use-script restores the old path, because the script remains the reference implementation.

On your two questions

The save was always going to be quick: --batch is 100, so it writes at most 99 buffered rows, and ex.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True) cancels the queued work rather than draining it. Only the handful of in-flight calls had to finish. Your experience matches.

And yes — the restart had to wait for the old process to exit, for a reason worth keeping in mind: two concurrent rdap runs would double the request rate against ARIN, which is the one thing that reliably produces the throttling bursts we saw earlier.
What to expect from the speedup

In the sandbox the native client did 20,000 IPs in 227s = 88 IPs/sec at 4 threads, against your previous 3.94 IPs/sec. I won't claim that multiple for your server — my path to ARIN is faster, so your gain will be smaller — but the first progress line will tell you immediately. Anything well above 3.94 is the connection reuse working, and at that point the remaining time is ARIN's actual response latency rather than handshakes.

Good news from the same code: the target query has NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ovt_places_usa_ip_trace t WHERE t.ip = p.ip_address), so the pass is resumable. Thought (20)

Decisive numbers. Three findings, one blocker.
4c-fix — unblock the deploy

The blocker is an untracked artifact, geo/landmarks_usa_rdap_errors.csv, the error CSV from the RDAP run. Move it out of the tree rather than delete it; it's data, and the deploy only cares that the tree is clean.

mv /home/boris/geo/src/claude/geo/landmarks_usa_rdap_errors.csv /home/boris/geo/landmarks_usa_rdap_errors.csv
cd /home/boris/geo/src/claude && ./geo/pipeline/deploy.sh

D2 verdict — Step 4 is essentially already done

onprem_v4_distinct 28,459 against 1,016 remaining means 27,443 addresses are already traced. Reading 1 holds. Skip 4d entirely; the pilot would measure throughput for a run that takes minutes.

4e — run after 4c succeeds

/var/trugeo/last_carrier_node/bin/last_carrier_node -source landmarks -landmark-table landmarks_usa -n 100000000 -concurrency 50

D4 — the real bottleneck, and it isn't the source list

Rule 2 kills 10,713,526 of 12.78M rows, 83.8%: the website's address belongs to a CDN, cloud or web host. Set against that, every rule that yields a landmark totals 131,601.

D3 puts a number on the five sources we added to beat the 48-ZIP result:
source	rows	on-prem addresses
osm	1,139,855	83
foursquare	275,517	50
wikidata	24,721	13
dotgov	14,149	4
nces_ipeds	6,075	9

1,460,317 rows produced 159 on-premises addresses, a yield of 0.011%. Overture's own yield is 0.206%, about 19x better per row. The national OSM import, 11.3GB and an hour of download, bought 83 addresses.

So the constraint is not how many landmark lists we have. Most organizations host their website off-premises, and no additional list of organizations changes that. This confirms what I flagged as the likely outcome: the method is at its ceiling, around 15,954 on-premises ZIPs from Overture.

D5 — the one number that settles whether the new sources were worth anything. Their 157 on-premises ZIPs may already be inside Overture's 15,954.

psql -d postgres -c "SELECT source, count(*) AS new_zips FROM (SELECT DISTINCT source, left(lpad(btrim(overture_zip),5,'0'),5) AS z FROM landmarks_usa WHERE onpremises AND source <> 'overture' AND overture_zip IS NOT NULL) d WHERE z NOT IN (SELECT left(lpad(btrim(overture_zip),5,'0'),5) FROM landmarks_usa WHERE onpremises AND source = 'overture' AND overture_zip IS NOT NULL) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;"

D6 — a discrepancy that must be resolved before Step 5

D4 computes 131,601 rows as on-premises. D1 says 120,352 are stored that way. The gap is 11,249, and you ran onpremises minutes ago, so stored and computed should agree.

I have two hypotheses and will not guess between them. Either a previous onpremises_hosting_rule.sql run set those rows false and they survived, or the chunked update skips rows whose ip_address is NULL while the dry run counts them.

psql -d postgres -c "SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE ip_address IS NULL) AS true_status_null_ip, count(*) FILTER (WHERE onpremises_reason LIKE 'hosting:%') AS hosting_reason_rows FROM landmarks_usa WHERE lookup_status = 'true';"

This matters because of something I verified in the code while checking the step order: the onpremises UPDATE is SET onpremises = {case} WHERE {cond} AND {base} AND ({case}) IS DISTINCT FROM t.onpremises, with no guard for hosting rows. Re-running Step 3's onpremises after Step 5's hosting rule silently reverts every hosting exclusion back to true. The hosting rule protects itself on the way in; the base step does not protect it on the way back. Treat Step 3 onpremises as something that must never run after Step 5 without re-running Step 5 after it.
Two code fixes I'd like to make

deploy.sh fails on untracked files that cannot affect a Go build, which is what just stopped you. Failing on untracked .go, go.mod and go.sum is defensible since a stray source file does get compiled in; failing on a CSV is not. I'd narrow the check and add the error CSV to .gitignore.

The onpremises step should preserve rows whose onpremises_reason starts with hosting:, closing the revert hazard above.

Both are small. Say the word and I'll put them up as a PR.

Next: 4c-fix, then 4e, and send D5 and D6. D5 tells us whether to stop adding sources; D6 gates Step 5.

D5 — source expansion is finished

6 new ZIPs. dotgov 2, foursquare 2, osm 2. From 1,460,317 rows across five sources. The national OSM import — 11.3GB, 20 minutes of download, an hour of filtering, 1.1M rows through RDAP — bought 2 ZIP codes.

D6 — both my hypotheses were wrong

true_status_null_ip = 0 and hosting_reason_rows = 0. Neither explanation survives, so I don't have one, and I'm not going to invent a third.

The useful consequence: hosting_reason_rows = 0 proves no hosting decisions exist yet, so re-running onpremises currently destroys nothing. That makes the direct test safe, and it also exercises the PR #65 change:

cd /home/boris/geo/src/claude && git pull origin main
cd geo && python3 overture_fetch/ovt_resolve_hosts.py onpremises --table landmarks_usa

If it reports roughly 11,249 rows changed, the earlier run was truncated and the chunked update isn't covering the table. If it reports 0 changed while the dry run still computes 131,601, then the update path and the rule disagree structurally and I'll go into ip_chunks.
The 4e trace found something worse than a count mismatch

Your on-premises landmark set contains Cloudflare. From the first twelve traces: 162.159.143.12, 104.21.91.100, 172.67.193.67, 104.20.35.60, 172.66.164.252. Those are Cloudflare anycast ranges. 104.18.x, 104.26.x, 172.64.x appear throughout, and the 172.68.52.x last hops confirm it — that's Cloudflare's own edge.

Cloudflare, Inc. is in provider_names, and rule 2 does precede the ISP rules in both the case and the rule expressions (I checked that the two are ordered identically). So the match is failing, and the reason matters: matching is exact equality on lower(btrim(registrant_1)). Any variant — a NetName like CLOUDFLARENET instead of the OrgName, or different punctuation — slips through and then qualifies under rule 3a or 4.

This is the one measurement I want most:

psql -d postgres -c "SELECT registrant_1, count(DISTINCT ip_address) AS ips FROM landmarks_usa WHERE onpremises GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 25;"

If CDN names dominate that list, the 28,459-address landmark set is substantially fake, 15,954 on-premises ZIPs is an overstatement, and fixing the match is worth more than any new data source. Note provider_names has 39 entries against isp_names's 1,100.
Your four questions

"Sparse ZIPs" — I was using it loosely, and the sloppiness hid something. I meant low-population ZIPs. The operational set is different: ZIPs with no on-premises landmark, which is roughly 28,000 of ~44,000. Those two sets correlate but are not the same, and the distinction decides the strategy. If a ZIP has no landmark because it has few businesses, more source lists cannot help — now proven at 6 ZIPs. But rule 2 killing 83.8% of all rows says the dominant cause isn't sparseness at all; it's that organizations host their websites off-premises, which happens in Manhattan as readily as in rural Montana. We have been solving the wrong problem.

DNS servers — better than my MX idea, with one caveat. For a domain already on Cloudflare the authoritative NS is usually Cloudflare too, so it adds nothing there. But for schools, local government and small institutions that run their own infrastructure, self-hosted authoritative DNS and mail are common, and both yield a hostname pointing at on-premises space. Your own trace output shows the pattern exists: mail.repairninja.com, mail.fairportny.com, ns1.racingchannel.com, dc1edge1.labattfood.com. Worth testing NS and MX together, plus vpn., remote., owa., portal. — but as a measured sample of rule-2-killed rows first, not a build.

nces_ipeds is not too small — it's the wrong population. IPEDS covers degree-granting postsecondary institutions, and ~6,000 is the right number. The tens of thousands you're thinking of are K-12: roughly 98,000 public schools. Those live in NCES CCD, which I rejected because its directory files carry addresses and NCES IDs but no website field — the search above confirms that's still true of the 2024-25 and 2025-26 releases. So CCD has the ZIP and lacks the website; the complement is domain enumeration. School districts cluster in .k12.<state>.us, and your trace caught one: autohost66-154-254-75.nwresd.k12.or.us. Certificate Transparency logs can enumerate hostnames under that suffix, then join to CCD on district name and state. The join is fuzzy and the yield is unknown, so this gets tested on one state before any national ingest. Given rule 2, 98,000 schools could still produce only a few hundred on-premises addresses.

Address-to-ZIP — use the Census geocoder, not Google, but it won't unlock much. The Census Bureau's Geocoding Services API takes batches of up to 10,000 records and 5MB, needs no API key, is free, and covers the US and territories. Google charges and restricts storing results. But on current evidence it buys little: dotgov already has 1,904 distinct ZIPs via the overture-zip locality fallback and still only 4 on-premises addresses, so better ZIPs would improve 4 records. CCD ships full addresses with ZIPs already. Missing ZIPs are not what's blocking us.

The discipline I'd draw from this round: every future source or evidence type gets a yield test on a sample before a national ingest. We just spent an 11.3GB download, 1.1M RDAP lookups and several hours to gain two ZIP codes, and a one-state pilot would have told us that in twenty minutes.

A rule question I am not going to decide for you

Cogent 2,739, Level 3 781, Hurricane Electric 705, NTT 411, Zayo 132 — about 4,768 addresses, roughly 17% of the landmark set. Those five sell IP transit to datacenters and colocation, not retail or business access lines. An address registered to Cogent is more likely in a colo cage than at a school. Rule 3a treats any isp_names match as proof of customer premises, and for backbone carriers that inference does not hold.

This is the same distinction as your existing transit_domain work, one layer up. Splitting isp_names into access carriers and transit carriers would cut the landmark set by up to 17% while removing addresses that are geographically wrong. I'd want your view before touching it, and the fan-out hosting rule in Step 5 may already catch most of them.
Your two directives

MX and NS. Measured, and the two are not comparable. MX found nothing on-premises in 4 of 4 districts — Google, Google, Mimecast, Microsoft — because schools have moved to Workspace and 365. NS returned the organisation's own ZIP in 2 of 4: City of Philadelphia at 19107, LAUSD at 90017.

One hazard this channel carries: nwresd.k12.or.us is Northwest Regional ESD, which serves many small Oregon districts. If small districts' DNS is run by a regional ESD or BOCES that self-hosts, every school in the consortium resolves to the ESD's ZIP, not its own. That is the fan-out problem again, and it would be invisible without the Step 5 hosting rule. Small rural districts are exactly our coverage gap, so this is where the channel is most likely to produce confidently wrong answers.

Four hand-picked large districts also bias optimistic — large districts self-host, small ones don't. The random sample settles it:

Public school domains, all available means. NCES CCD is the ZIP anchor: ~98,000 schools and ~19,000 districts with name, address, ZIP and NCES ID, and no website field in the 2024-25 or 2025-26 releases. The domains have to come from elsewhere, in descending expected yield:

State education agency directories are first, because several publish a website column alongside the address, which means ZIP and domain arrive together with no join at all. California's public schools file carries one. Fifty sources, but each is small and authoritative.

Certificate Transparency against .k12.<state>.us is second. Every TLS certificate issued under that suffix is public, and the live test proved schools live there: dns1.phila.k12.pa.us.

NS records are third and bootstrap the other two — lausd.org led to ns1.lausd.net, philasd.org led to dns1.phila.k12.pa.us. Each domain found yields more domains.

Then the .gov list we already hold, since some districts have migrated.

If that number is small, we stop, and we'll have spent a day instead of the 11.3GB download and 1.1M RDAP lookups that bought 2 ZIP codes.

The transit carriers: I withdraw the question, and your reframing is why

Your point reframes it correctly. I was reasoning about what those carriers sell in general — transit to datacenters — rather than what a specific address is doing. Cogent, Level 3, Hurricane Electric, NTT and Zayo supply dedicated access to university and corporate campuses, and campus housing plus at-work viewing is residential-equivalent traffic at a known location. For this pipeline's purpose that is a landmark, not noise.

The composition of the on-premises set supports that directly: provider_names.sql already documents keeping University of Hawaii, the University System of New Hampshire, Northwestern Memorial, UPMC and Baptist Health for the same reason — they hold their own space and serve real people from it.

There's a second reason to withdraw, which I should have seen before raising it. My question was an instance of one already settled: exclude by registrant name, or by per-address behaviour. The standing decision is per-address, because per-registrant naming would have destroyed 651 on-premises places to exclude 17. Splitting isp_names into access and transit tiers is that same mistake in new clothing — it would drop up to 4,768 addresses wholesale to catch whichever subset actually sits in colos.

The fan-out rule already distinguishes them and needs no list: a campus DIA address serves one ZIP cluster, a colo address serves disjoint ones. After Step 5 this reads the answer straight off:

psql -d postgres -c "SELECT registrant, count(*) AS addresses, count(*) FILTER (WHERE verdict LIKE 'hosting:%') AS called_hosting, count(*) FILTER (WHERE verdict LIKE 'on-premises:%') AS kept, round(avg(clusters_at_address), 2) AS mean_clusters FROM address_hosting_tbl WHERE registrant IN ('Cogent Communications, LLC','Level 3 Parent, LLC','Hurricane Electric LLC','NTT America, Inc.','Zayo Bandwidth') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;"

If those come back mostly single-cluster, rule 3a was right and nothing needs changing. If they fan out, the hosting rule has already removed them without anyone writing a name list.

The 7 addresses are a textbook case of the failure mode the file already documents

15 rows, 7 distinct addresses. Every Microsoft one is Azure space registered to ZIP 98052, Redmond. The landmarks are Seattle-area businesses — restaurants, a temple, an insurance agent — with sites hosted on Azure, sitting in 98005, 98008, 98033, 98034, 98052 and 98053. Those are Redmond's own ZIP or adjacent to it, so they passed rule 4 or rule 5 on the strength of being near Microsoft's head office. The Amazon case is the same shape: registrant ZIP 20124 against landmark 22192, both Virginia, so adjacency carried it.

provider_names.sql predicted this exactly: placing the exclusion after the ZIP tests "would let any landmark that happens to sit near a provider's registered office through: Akamai in Cambridge, Cloudflare and Fastly in San Francisco, Amazon in Herndon." Microsoft in Redmond is the same pattern with a name that wasn't on the list. PR #67 is confirmed correct.

One side observation worth noting: vedatemple.org appears four times with ZIP 98052 and 98053 across overture and osm, and saharamediterraneankitchen.com twice. The same place from two sources disagrees about its ZIP. At 7 addresses that's immaterial, but ZIP disagreement between sources feeds directly into the adjacency rule, so it may matter at scale.
The carrier question: we were each partly right, and the per-address rule is quantifiably the right design

4,813 addresses across those five carriers. 1,316 called hosting (27.3%), 3,497 kept.

Your reframing holds: the clear majority are genuine institutional premises, and the name-list split I floated would have destroyed 3,497 real landmarks to catch the rest. My concern wasn't baseless either — a quarter of them do behave like shared hosting, ranging from Level 3 at 34.3% down to Zayo at 15.0%.

What settles it is that the fan-out rule separates them per address, with no name list at all. A 3,497-to-1,316 split is the same lesson as the 651-to-17 case that killed registrant-name exclusion the first time. That generalises: when a registrant mixes uses, measure the address, never the name.

Caveat on those numbers. address_hosting_tbl was built from landmarks_usa when onpremises = true was 120,352; it is now 131,601. And onpremises_reason is still zero rows, so onpremises_hosting_rule.sql has not been applied. The percentages above are indicative only and need rebuilding on the corrected set.
