California: schema verified, yield not measured, download blocked

One fetch succeeded — 8,796,076 bytes, tab-delimited, 46 fields. The ones that matter: Zip, WebSite, StatusType, District, School, Street, City, Latitude, Longitude, LastUpDate, and NCESDist plus NCESSchool. Those last two are better than I expected: the state file carries the federal identifiers, so CCD becomes a clean key-join for coverage checking with no name matching at all.

Then the endpoint began returning a Radware captcha and has stayed blocked, including with a browser user-agent, so I could not count how many active schools have a usable website. I'm not going to estimate it.

Two consequences. The loader cannot depend on fetching; it needs an --input path for a locally downloaded file, the way osm-pbf already works. And the file needs QUOTE_NONE parsing — stray " characters in unquoted fields collapsed 8.8MB to 73 rows when I first read it, which would have silently discarded almost everything.

From your box, which has a residential IP:

cd /home/boris/geo && curl -sS -L -o pubschls.txt "https://www.cde.ca.gov/schooldirectory/report?rid=dl1&tp=txt"

' | head -25
awk -F'\t' 'NR>1 && $4=="Active" && $21 ~ /\./ && $11 != "" {n++} END {print "active with website and ZIP:", n}' pubschls.txt

If that returns roughly 8.8MB and a real count, I'll write the loader against the actual file rather than against my assumptions about it.

"adjacency carried it": Adjacency should never be applied BETWEEN registrants, only WITHIN a registrant. It is intended to set onpremises=true in two cases: (1) a customer registrant served from a node in an adjacent ZIP code (common occurrence in rural areas); and (2) a provider registrant's own office, such as Cloudlare's in San Francisco (here the office should count as an onpremises=true landmark ONLY if the ZIP code is the same between that registrant's RDAP record and the landmark; adjacency for that registrant should not set onpremises=true and should not ever be applied to the other registrant, if such exists).

"Then re-run the fan-off verification query to get real percentages": Reissue that code. Asking me to rerun unlabeled code invites error.

Your adjacency objection is correct, and I can point at the line

Verified in cmd_onpremises:

adj_test = EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM {adj_t} adj WHERE adj.a = {ovz} AND adj.b IN ({z1}, {z2}))

adj.b IN (z1, z2) tests the landmark ZIP against either registrant's ZIP with no regard for which registrant it came from. Registrant 1's identity plus registrant 2's ZIP carries the row. That is precisely the between-registrant application you are ruling out. Rule 4 has the same shape, ovz IN (z1, z2).

It has been masked until now only because rule 2 short-circuits any provider row to false before adjacency is reached — which means your case (2) is not implemented at all. A provider's own office is currently always false, never true on exact match.

Faithful implementation of your spec, in order:

    registrant_1 IS NULL → NULL
    no landmark ZIP → NULL
    all registrants are ISPs → true
    landmark ZIP exactly equals any non-ISP registrant's ZIP, provider included → true
    no provider registrant present, and landmark ZIP is adjacent to that same registrant's ZIP, evaluated per registrant and only for non-ISP non-provider registrants → true
    otherwise false

One objection before I build it. Step 4 reintroduces the failure we just diagnosed. The Azure landmarks were restaurants and a temple in 98052 — Redmond, Microsoft's registered ZIP — hosted on Azure. Exact ZIP match makes those true, because any business sitting in a provider's HQ ZIP and hosted by that provider matches exactly. Redmond, Cambridge, San Francisco and Herndon are commercial ZIPs full of such businesses. Exact matching narrows the hazard that provider_names.sql documents; it does not remove it.

The distinguishing evidence is fan-out, not ZIP: a provider's content space serves many disjoint ZIPs, a provider's corporate office serves one. So the hosting rule may already recover genuine provider offices without an exact-ZIP exception.

The reason prefix8 fails here specifically: in this corpus the discriminating token comes after a long common prefix. Your own section-2 output is dominated by University of X, City of X, State of X. Eight characters captures universi, city of , state of and throws the distinguishing word away. It also cannot do the thing you wanted it for — LAUSD and Los Angeles Unified School District share no prefix at all, so abbreviation expansion is untouched.

And the Google row shows how accidental its one success is. google l versus google f differ at character 8. At seven characters both are google and Google's hosting merges with Google Fiber, destroying the distinction we established two turns ago.

Rare-token scoring 11/14 points at the right principle: the discriminating information is in the rare tokens, not the prefix and not overall string similarity. But my own matcher merged Google LLC with Google Fiber Inc., because I had put fiber in the common-token list. That is the honest warning: the stopword list is itself a tuning parameter, and getting it wrong reproduces the exact failure being avoided. I would build a checked-in labelled pair set first and run it on every change, before trusting any matcher in the rule.
Two things I need from you before changing the rule

What is being matched? I read "matched between RDAP and landmark records" as the RDAP registrant name against the landmark's own name, so that name identity proves the organisation holds its own address regardless of ZIP. That would be a new and strong rule, and it is directly useful for schools — CDE gives the school and district names, RDAP gives the registrant, and a match proves the school holds its space. "Abbreviation expansion" fits that reading. The other possible reading is matching registrants against isp_names and provider_names, where the answer is different: those lists are curated, and exact matching is working at 39 names rejecting 10.7M rows with 7 leaks.

The between-registrant case. Looking again, adj.b IN (z1, z2) expands to adj.b = z1 OR adj.b = z2, so each disjunct already pairs the landmark ZIP with one registrant's own ZIP. I cannot see it crossing registrants, and I don't want to restructure the core rule on my guess at your intent. Which registrant supplies the identity and which the ZIP in the case you have in mind?

One defect I can see and will fix regardless: z1/z2 null an ISP's ZIP but not a provider's. Rule 2 makes that unreachable today, but when a provider's name is an unmatched variant — Microsoft Corp — rule 2 doesn't fire and adjacency then uses the provider's ZIP. That is precisely how the Redmond landmarks at 98005, 98008, 98033 and 98034 became on-premises.
California, with one hazard I caught in time

8,816 active schools carrying both a website and a ZIP. The loader requires --input because the CDE endpoint answers a datacenter address with a captcha served as HTTP 200, which a downloading loader would parse as data and report success on. It parses with QUOTE_NONE, without which the 8.8MB file collapses to 73 rows silently.

It also reports the shared-host waste before anything is spent: schools usually publish the district's site, so one address at the district office carries schools in many ZIPs, and node_fanout.sql will correctly reject it as hosting. The hosts serving one ZIP are the real candidates.

Do not run migrate_into_landmarks_usa.sql. Decomposed, each step labelled, each bounded, none of them able to hang silently. Merge the four PRs first — --dry-run and the timing changes are in #68.

C0 — clear the ground. Your earlier output ended at a (END) pager prompt four times. A psql sitting at a pager inside a transaction holds its locks and the next writer queues behind it with no output. Press q in any open psql, then confirm nothing is holding anything:

psql -d postgres -c "SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, left(query, 50) AS query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE pid <> pg_backend_pid() AND (state <> 'idle' OR xact_start IS NOT NULL) ORDER BY xact_start NULLS LAST;"
psql -d postgres -c "SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, left(query, 50) AS query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;"

Both should come back empty. The second returning rows means something is blocked and names the holder.

C1 — parse only, no database connection at all. This is the step that separates a file problem from a database problem. Verified by replacing require_table, load_rows and psql with functions that raise: the dry run completes without calling any of them.

Thought (3)

8,816 loaded in 0.8 seconds, and the shape is far better than the dotgov/OSM precedent: 4,839 of 5,165 hosts serve exactly one ZIP, 1,367 distinct ZIPs, 32.9% shared-host waste.
One limitation of my own measurement, before you spend RDAP on this

That analysis counts hostnames, and the fan-out hazard operates on addresses. School-website vendors — Edlio, Finalsite, Apptegy, SchoolMessenger — give every school its own hostname while serving them all from a handful of IPs. So 4,839 distinct single-ZIP hostnames can collapse to a few dozen addresses, each carrying schools across the whole state.

32.9% is therefore a floor on the waste, not an estimate of it. The real number only exists after resolve, and resolve is DNS only, so it costs nothing to find out before committing RDAP budget. I'd rather find this now than discover it in node_fanout.sql after hours of lookups, which is the mistake the last five sources made.

C5 — the measurement that decides whether to continue

Three queries, all cheap because they are scoped to 8,816 rows.

psql -d postgres -c "SELECT count(*) AS rows, count(*) FILTER (WHERE ip_address IS NOT NULL) AS resolved, count(DISTINCT ip_address) AS distinct_ips, count(DISTINCT left(lpad(btrim(postcode),5,'0'),5)) AS zips FROM landmarks_usa WHERE source = 'ca_cde';"
psql -d postgres -c "SELECT zips_per_ip, count(*) AS ips, sum(places) AS places FROM (SELECT ip_address, count(DISTINCT left(lpad(btrim(postcode),5,'0'),5)) AS zips_per_ip, count(*) AS places FROM landmarks_usa WHERE source = 'ca_cde' AND ip_address IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1) d GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;"
psql -d postgres -c "SELECT ip_address, count(DISTINCT left(lpad(btrim(postcode),5,'0'),5)) AS zips, count(*) AS places, min(website) AS example_site FROM landmarks_usa WHERE source = 'ca_cde' AND ip_address IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 20;"

The second query is the decisive one. zips_per_ip = 1 rows are genuine single-school landmarks and will survive the fan-out rule. Everything above 1 is vendor hosting that will be rejected, correctly. The third names the vendors, and any of them that turn out to carry hundreds of schools are candidates for provider_names — which would spare the RDAP cost on every other state when we get there.

Hold before rdap. If the addresses concentrate badly, the right move is to add the vendors to provider_names first and only look up what can survive.

The stake, for calibration: the last five sources cost 1.46M rows and an 11.3GB download and returned 6 new ZIPs. California is offering 1,367 ZIPs before attrition. Even heavy losses here beat that comfortably, which is why it's worth measuring carefully rather than either abandoning or rushing.

A correction to my own instruction

My loader prints that the locality fallback is not needed for California. True, but it reads as though overture-zip can be skipped. It cannot: overture-zip is the step that copies postcode into overture_zip and labels it overture_zip_source='postcode', and onpremises reads overture_zip only. Skip it and every California row falls into rule 1 as NULL.
S1 — the decisive question, before the chain

Of the ZIPs reachable from surviving addresses, how many are ones we do not already cover? If most are already in the 9,728, California adds little whatever the chain does.

This is the one slow query — it scans landmarks_usa to build the covered set and takes a few minutes. It is read-only and writes nothing.

psql -d postgres -c "WITH covered AS (SELECT DISTINCT left(lpad(btrim(overture_zip),5,'0'),5) AS zip FROM landmarks_usa WHERE onpremises AND overture_zip IS NOT NULL), single_ip AS (SELECT ip_address FROM landmarks_usa WHERE source = 'ca_cde' AND ip_address IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(DISTINCT left(lpad(btrim(postcode),5,'0'),5)) = 1), cand AS (SELECT DISTINCT left(lpad(btrim(l.postcode),5,'0'),5) AS zip FROM landmarks_usa l JOIN single_ip s ON s.ip_address = l.ip_address WHERE l.source = 'ca_cde') SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM cand) AS candidate_zips, (SELECT count(*) FROM cand c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM covered v WHERE v.zip = c.zip)) AS new_zips;"

S2 — the chain, which is nearly free here

556 distinct addresses, most already in the RDAP cache from the 15.2M-row corpus. The lookups are seconds, not hours.

cd /home/boris/geo/src/claude/geo && python3 overture_fetch/ovt_resolve_hosts.py rdap --table landmarks_usa
python3 overture_fetch/ovt_resolve_hosts.py registrants --table landmarks_usa
python3 overture_fetch/ovt_resolve_hosts.py overture-zip --table landmarks_usa
python3 overture_fetch/ovt_resolve_hosts.py onpremises --table landmarks_usa

An operational point for the other 49 states

Your resolve run spent roughly four minutes in whole-table scans to resolve 2,414 new hosts. That cost is fixed per chain step and independent of how few rows are new, and there are four steps. Running the chain once per state would pay it fifty times over for no benefit.

So once California's yield is known, ingest every state's directory first and run the chain once across all of them. If S1 says the new-ZIP gain is real, that is the next build: a state-directory loader covering the states that publish a website column, rather than fifty separate chain runs.

For calibration against the last attempt: five sources, 1.46M rows, an 11.3GB download, 6 new ZIPs. California alone is offering up to 379 candidate ZIPs before overlap. S1 tells us how many of those are actually new.

Matching: the choices

There are three distinct matching problems in this pipeline. They get conflated because they all compare organisation names, but they have different inputs, different failure costs, and different right answers.
(A) Registrant against a reference list

What it is: registrant_1 compared to isp_names (1,101 entries) and provider_names (42). Decides rule 2 (provider → hard false) and rule 3 (all-ISP → hard true). Currently exact equality on lower(btrim(name)).

Why exact matching works here, and it is not luck. Both sides come from the same vocabulary. Those lists were populated from observed ARIN registrant strings, so they are not independent renderings of a name — they are copies of what ARIN returns. Measured: 42 provider names reject 10,713,526 of 12,799,143 rows. The entire residue was 7 addresses, from two organisations holding multiple ARIN org records under different spellings (Microsoft Corp alongside Microsoft Corporation).

Why loosening it is dangerous. Google LLC is Google's hosting and must be excluded; Google Fiber Inc. is a retail ISP and must not be. Verified by RDAP: 8.8.8.8, the GCP load balancer, the mail edge and the googledomains nameserver all return Google LLC, while 136.33.1.1 returns Google Fiber Inc. Prefix-8 separates them only because they happen to differ at character 8. At seven characters both are google and the distinction is destroyed.

Recommendation: keep exact matching. The maintenance cost is a few names per large ingest, and they surface automatically by ranking registrants that remain on-premises — that is how Microsoft Corp and Interactive Educational Services were found. A feedback loop with evidence beats a fuzzy matcher with none.
(B) Registrant against the landmark's own name

What it is: if ARIN says an address belongs to "Los Angeles Unified School District" and the landmark is that district, the organisation holds its own address. This is not implemented today.

What it buys. Evidence independent of ZIP. Rules 4 and 5 currently need the registrant's postal ZIP to equal or adjoin the landmark's, which proves proximity. Name identity proves ownership, which is strictly stronger. It would also rescue the case where ARIN lists a corporate or district-office ZIP while the landmark sits in a neighbouring one — today that lands in rule 5 at best and rule 6b at worst. For schools it fits well: district names are distinctive, and a self-hosting district's ARIN record carries its name. LAUSD's own nameserver ns1.lausd.net resolved to 204.108.64.10 registered to "Los Angeles Unified School District" at 90017.

What it risks, and why the risk is higher than in (A). This compares two independent renderings — CDE writes one form, ARIN another, and neither is derived from the other. Exact matching cannot work, so a fuzzy matcher is required, and that is precisely where the measured failures live. A false positive here does not merely misclassify: it asserts on-premises and pushes a ZIP into the final product. Merging "University of Hawaii" with "University of Minnesota" would hand a Honolulu address to a Minneapolis ZIP.
(C) Landmark against landmark, across sources

Not what you asked, but it exists and I should name it: vedatemple.org appears four times under ZIPs 98052 and 98053 across overture and osm. The unified table keys on (source, source_id), so cross-source duplicates coexist and can disagree about ZIP, which then feeds the adjacency test. Separate problem, and I would leave it alone for now.
The matchers, measured

Fourteen real pairs taken from your own registrant output:
matcher	correct	how it fails
prefix 8, lowercase	7/14	merges University of Hawaii with Minnesota, City of San Antonio with Houston, STATE OF DELAWARE with South Carolina, University of Illinois with Kansas
trigram similarity ≥ 0.60	8/14	same class of failure
rare-token	11/14	merged Google LLC with Google Fiber

Why prefix length is the wrong dial. The discriminating word sits after a long shared prefix. "University of " is 14 characters; "City of " is 8. Any fixed prefix captures the shared part and discards the distinguishing one. Overall string similarity fails identically, because "University of Hawaii" and "University of Minnesota" share most of their characters. Lengthening the prefix doesn't fix it either — it just breaks the matches you wanted, which is why prefix-8 also failed "University of California Davis Medical Center" against "UC Davis Medical Center".

What the corpus actually demands. Weight the rare tokens. Strip corporate suffixes and the high-frequency institutional words — university, city, state, county, school, district, of, the — then require a shared rare token and no conflicting one. hawaii against minnesota conflicts, so no match. charter communications inc against charter communications llc shares charter with nothing conflicting, so match. Acronyms need separate handling, because LAUSD and Los Angeles Unified School District share no token at all; compare the initials of the significant tokens.

The caveat that matters most. My rare-token matcher failed on the single most important pair in the corpus, Google LLC against Google Fiber Inc., because I had listed fiber as a common token. The stopword list is itself a tuning parameter, and getting it wrong reproduces exactly the error the matcher exists to prevent. So a labelled pair set, checked in and run on every change with that pair as a required non-match, has to come before the matcher — not after.
What I would do

Keep (A) exact. Build (B), but in this order: regression set first, then the matcher, then measure how many rows it would flip before wiring it into the rule. Record its verdicts under their own onpremises_reason value so the contribution is auditable and revertible, the way the hosting rule is.

And one constraint regardless of how good the matcher gets: (B) must never override rule 2. If the landmark is Cloudflare's own San Francisco office and ARIN says Cloudflare, name matching would correctly call it on-premises — and it would still be useless, because the carrier node adjacent to that address is Cloudflare's edge router, which routes content and never subscribers. Correct and unusable are different things, and that is the same argument provider_names.sql already makes in its header.

Est. Credits Used: 3.72

Elapsed Time: 1m 27s

The prefix-8 matching I suggested for discussion was intended only for the determination of whether adjacency is acceptable — for which purpose the registrant whose ZIP code we check must be the same and the landmark owner. Such a match can never be guaranteed to be 100% accurate. It should not be used in any other registrant name matching, especially where both fields are ARIN-reported. For the adjacency test, use "Weight the rare tokens" but exclude critically differentiating terms such as "Fiber" from the common-token list. Alternatively, identify the OTHER registrant by membership in either the isp_names or the provider_names table. The remaining registrant will then be deemed to be the same as the landmark regardless of the actual string of its name (so "Los Angeles Unified School District" will match "LAUSD". This approach fails on registrants deliberately omitted from either table (Southwest Cyberport and Synergy Networks) and any new companies (by the way, explain your plan to catch them and classify them as ISPs or providers). Critique these two options. If necessary, run a test to identify the better one, but after you ingest the public-school data from the rest of the country.

unclassified_hosting_candidates.sql

Ran command

Your clarification changes what the defect is, and I had it wrong.
The actual defect in rule 5

I was looking for a registrant_1-versus-registrant_2 pairing error. There isn't one — adj.b IN (z1, z2) already pairs the landmark ZIP with one registrant's ZIP at a time. The real defect is that nothing establishes that the ZIP-supplying registrant is the landmark's owner at all.

That matters asymmetrically between the two rules. Rule 4 is partly self-validating: if a registrant's ZIP equals the landmark's ZIP, the proximity is exact and ownership matters less. Rule 5 stretches the claim to a neighbouring ZIP, and that stretch is only legitimate under your reasoning — a rural owner whose registered address sits one ZIP over. If the registrant is a stranger, adjacency is coincidence, and in a dense metro it is coincidence that fires constantly. Microsoft's 98052 against landmarks in 98005, 98008, 98033 and 98034 is that failure with a real count attached.

So adjacency needs an ownership gate. Both your options are ways to build one.
Option 1, name matching with rare tokens

It fails safe. A false negative loses one legitimate adjacency, costing coverage. A false positive requires the registrant's name to actually resemble the landmark's, which an unrelated vendor's rarely does — Interactive Educational Services will not rare-token-match Alpine County Office of Education. The errors land on the conservative side.

It works on single-registrant rows, which is nearly everything. 12,799,143 rows have registrant_1; only 215,761 have registrant_2. 98.3% of rows have exactly one registrant.

Excluding "Fiber" from the common-token list is right but doesn't generalise. I put fiber there and merged Google LLC with Google Fiber. The lesson isn't "also keep fiber" — it's that the stopword list is a tuning parameter with no principled membership test, so it needs a checked-in labelled pair set with Google LLC/Google Fiber as a required non-match, running on every change. The list is only safe if something enforces it.

The real problem with Option 1 is the landmark name, not the matcher. For schools, the landmark name is the school and the ARIN registrant is usually the district. Encinal High against Alameda Unified School District shares no rare token, so Option 1 fails on exactly the population we are building for. CDE gives us the district name — and my loader throws it away. COLUMNS in lm_fetch.py has no district field, and cmd_ca_cde uses District only as a fallback when School is blank. That has to be fixed before Option 1 can be tested on schools at all.
Option 2, ownership by elimination

Its strength is that it needs no string comparison, so LAUSD matching Los Angeles Unified School District is free, which is precisely where Option 1 struggles.

Its error mode is unsafe, and that is the decisive difference. An unclassified third party is presumed to be the landmark owner, so adjacency fires on the host's ZIP. That is the Redmond failure again, reached by presumption rather than by spelling variant — and the population of unclassified vendors is unbounded and grows with every new ingest. Option 1 errs toward missing landmarks; Option 2 errs toward inventing them.

On your named exceptions it fails conservatively, not dangerously. Southwest Cyberport is in isp_names, so its ZIP is nulled and it cannot be the presumed owner. For its genuine access customers the real owner is the subscriber, who has no ARIN record at all, so no adjacency is possible. That loses true positives rather than creating false ones — the acceptable direction.
What I would build: both, in series

Elimination as a necessary condition, name match as the sufficient one.

A registrant in either table is never the owner, so its ZIP is excluded from adjacency — that is Option 2's safe half, and it also closes the gap where z1/z2 currently null ISP ZIPs but not provider ZIPs. A registrant in neither table becomes a candidate owner, and adjacency fires only if the name also matches the landmark or its district. Rule 4 keeps needing neither, since exact proximity is its own evidence.

That way an unclassified vendor fails the name test and gets no adjacency, while a district whose name matches passes. Option 2 alone would admit the vendor; Option 1 alone would reject the district whose name we discarded.
Catching and classifying new companies

PR #72 makes this a query rather than a plan. node_fanout.sql already records, per address, whether it serves disjoint ZIP clusters and which registrant holds it — so an unknown hosting company is already visible as a registrant with hosting: verdicts and no membership in either list. That is exactly how Interactive Educational Services surfaced, at 54 ZIPs and 125 schools from one address, ranked beside Cloudflare and Fastly.

It reports three things: unclassified registrants by ZIP spread, what excluding each would cost in on-premises addresses, and how much of the registrant population the lists cover. The second matters because a mixed business belongs in neither table — Southwest Cyberport appeared in this same ranking and is an ISP.

Two rules are in the file header because they are easy to get wrong. Read what the company says it does before listing it. And take the name string from RDAP rather than retyping it, because both lists match exactly and only work because they are copies of what ARIN returns.

Detection after the fact is acceptable because two independent mechanisms reject a new vendor — the name list, which needs maintenance, and the per-address fan-out rule, which does not and caught this one unaided.
Order of work, per your instruction

Ingest the rest of the country first, then test the two options. Two things stand between here and that ingest:

The state files need your browser. Texas 404'd from the sandbox and New York failed TLS, and California served exactly one file before switching to captchas permanently. The routes are AskTED's statewide "School and District File with Site Address" and the NYSED "Directory of Public and Non-Public Schools and Administrators".

And lm_fetch.py must start storing the district name, or Option 1 cannot be tested on schools regardless of how good the matcher is. I'd rather fix that while ingesting than discover it during the test.

You're right about the matcher, and the reason is sharper than I had it

I had Option 1 failing safe. It doesn't — its false negatives concentrate exactly where adjacency matters most.

A high school occupies one ZIP, so if the matcher fails to connect Encinal High to Alameda Unified School District, adjacency is denied and nothing of value is lost: the address really is at the district office, not the school, so the landmark was never legitimate. Harmless, as you say.

But a university or hospital system legitimately owns addresses across many ZIPs under one registrant. John A. Burns School of Medicine shares no rare token with University of Hawaii, so the matcher denies adjacency for a site the institution genuinely owns, in its own ZIP, where adjacency is the correct call. The false negatives land on multi-ZIP institutions and are invisible — a rejected landmark leaves no trace.

Option 2's errors are the opposite shape. An unclassified third party presumed to be the owner will be serving landmarks across many ZIPs, which is precisely the fan-out signature, so node_fanout.sql catches it downstream. Its one uncaught case is the single-landmark provider address — Webflow's 99 places on one address in one ZIP scored on-premises: single zip and only provider_names stopped it.

So the comparison inverts: Option 2's failures are largely recoverable, Option 1's are not. Elimination plus the fan-out rule plus provider_names for the single-landmark blind spot is the better gate, and name matching adds little. I'd drop it rather than build it, and revisit only if the national ingest leaves a large rule-6b reject population concentrated in multi-ZIP institutions — which is measurable after the fact.

Running the probe on it found three defects I would not have found any other way. School Zip didn't match my anchored ^zip, so the probe would have called the better of the two files unusable. Taking one column per role would have read the district's ZIP against the school's website. And fixing the status pattern re-broke California's StatusType, caught only because I re-ran the fixture.

That changes the division of labour: Socrata and ArcGIS portals are machine-fetchable from here, so I should survey those myself before asking you for anything. Texas proves it works, and I was about to hand you a manual job for a state that needed none.
